CLEAN Soil Air Water Renewables Sustainability Environmental Monitoring Research Article Influence of Crude Oil on Denitrification in Subtidal Sediments in the Northern Gulf of Mexico In this study the impact of hydrocarbons on nitrogen cycling in intertidal sediments from a barrier island in the north central Gulf of Mexico was investigated. Initial total petroleum hydrocarbon (TPH) concentrations of the sediments averaged \(49 \pm 27\ \mathrm{mg\ kg}^{-1}\) in June and \(75 \pm 48\ \mathrm{mg\ kg}^{-1}\) in November. Following the addition of crude oil, TPH concentrations increased to \(340 \pm 73\) and \(296 \pm 50\ \mathrm{mg\ kg}^{-1}\) in June and November, respectively. Sediment oxygen demand (SOD), inorganic nitrogen and phosphorus fluxes, and denitrification capacity, measured with the isotope pairing technique (IPT) within a week of oiling, were consistently higher in June compared to rates in November when temperatures were \(10^{\circ}\mathrm{C}\) lower. Despite significantly higher TPH concentrations in the oiled treatments, SOD, nutrient fluxes, nitrogen fixation, denitrification, and anammox, did not differ between the treatments. Potential denitrification rates, measured in the presence of excess nitrate (100 \(\mu\)M), were similar between the control and oil treatments, but significantly higher than rates measured with the IPT. The elevated rates of potential denitrification suggest the presence of an active extant microbial community capable of significant attenuation of porewater nitrate concentrations. The insignificant changes in nitrogen cycling in response to petroleum hydrocarbon additions at a site with hydrocarbons present, albeit at low concentrations, suggests resiliency in nitrogen cycling in response to additional hydrocarbon inputs in ranges investigated in this study. Keywords: Denitrification; Isotope pairing technique; Marine sediments; Nitrogen fixation; Total petroleum hydrocarbons Received: August 10, 2016; revised: December 12, 2016; accepted: June 7, 2017 DOI: 10.1002/clen.201600546 1 Introduction In the aftermath of an oil spill, the abundance of the microbial communities capable of metabolizing petroleum hydrocarbons as a carbon source increases [1]. But because of the overabundance of carbon relative to nitrogen or phosphorus in hydrocarbons, there is an increase in demand for inorganic nutrients, especially nitrogen, by microorganisms capable of degrading hydrocarbons [2]. Changes in three microbially driven processes following oil spills, namely nitrogen fixation, denitrification, and anammox, can affect the availability of nitrogen in sediments. As opposed to nitrogen fixation, which supplies bioavailable nitrogen to the sediments, denitrification and anammox transform bioavailable nitrogen to dinitrogen (\(\mathrm{N}_2\)) gas that is then lost to the atmosphere. While denitrification and anammox both result in the production of dinitrogen gas, denitrification is the dissimilatory process by which nitrate or nitrite is used as electron acceptors [3], whereas anammox is the anaerobic oxidation of ammonium with nitrite serving as the terminal electron acceptor [4]. Understanding changes in these processes following an oil spill is of particular interest because of their impact on nitrogen availability and how they can affect hydrocarbon degradation. Previous investigations have shown that changes in rates of nitrogen fixation [5] or denitrification [6–10] depend on the quantity and quality of the oil and habitat type where an oil spill occurs. Potential denitrification rates in marsh and coastal sediments exposed to crude oil, for example, were lower, and the decline in rates were much more pronounced the longer the sediments were exposed to crude oil [6, 7], or when the sediments were exposed to fresh crude as opposed to weathered oil [7]. However, because denitrification is an anaerobic process, others have suggested that following exposure to hydrocarbons and reduced oxygen availability in the sediments, denitrification would be enhanced. For example, in contaminated sediments within the vicinity of the Deepwater Horizon (DWH) accident site, and in naturally occurring oil seeps in the Gulf of Mexico, Scott et al. [8] noted a shift in the metabolic flow of nitrogen to the denitrification pathways. Similarly, laboratory experiments have demonstrated that following oil contamination in marsh sediments mineralization and potential denitrification rates increased, and these increases were attributed to the enhanced supply of carbon from the oil [9], and a change in redox conditions that favored denitrification [8, 10]. Our goal was to determine how oiling with weathered crude oil changes nitrogen cycling, particularly denitrification, nitrogen fixation and anammox, in a coastal region. Current strategies for remediation of oiled beaches and wetlands include application of nitrogen and/or nitrogen and phosphorus [11, 12] with the ultimate goal of keeping porewater bioavailable nutrient concentrations at levels that are adequate for the microbial community capable of hydrocarbon degradation [13, 14]. A better understanding of the impact of hydrocarbons on nitrogen cycling in marine sediments can lead to better predictions of the impacts of oil spills on biogeochemical cycles and improved remediation strategies of impacted ecosystems. 2 Materials and methods 2.1 Study site Samples were collected in June and November 2014 from a subtidal sandy site on the east end of Dauphin Island, AL, USA (30°15′3″N, 88°4′40″W); a barrier island located in the northern Gulf of Mexico (Fig. 1). Point measurements of temperature, salinity, and dissolved oxygen were recorded with a YSI 556 Multiparameter Meter during each sampling event. 10 mL of site water was collected in triplicate and filtered through a GF/F (0.7 μm pore size) and frozen until analyses were performed for dissolved inorganic nitrogen (DIN: NO\(_2^-\), NO\(_3^-\), NO\(_4^-\)) and PO\(_4^{3-}\) with standard wet chemical techniques modified for the Skalar SAN\(^+\) Autoanalyzer. 2.2 Porewater nutrients Sediments were collected in triplicate with a 2.6 cm id corer and sectioned in 1 cm segments to a depth of 6 cm for the determination of total extractable porewater nutrients. Nutrients were extracted with 10 mL of 1 M NaCl [15] after shaking at 60 rpm on a shaker table for 4 h. Samples were then centrifuged at 4500 rpm for 10 min and the supernatant was GF/F filtered and frozen for analysis for DIN and PO\(_4^{3-}\) as described above. 2.3 Chlorophyll-\( \alpha \) (chl-\( \alpha \)) Samples for sediment chl-\( \alpha \) concentrations were collected in triplicate with a corer (1.4 cm id) to a depth of 1 cm. Sediment wet weights were recorded prior to being stored at –80°C. Sediments were freeze-dried, dry weight was recorded, and were extracted in 10 mL of 90% acetone for 24 h. Both surface water and sediment chl-\( \alpha \) concentrations were determined fluorometrically [16]. 2.4 Crude oil weathering and analysis The crude oil was weathered by placing an aliquot of Louisiana sweet crude oil in an open container on a mechanical shaker at ca. 85 rpm for five days under a fume-hood in a dark environment. Total petroleum hydrocarbons (THP) in the sediments were extracted according to the EPA SW-846-3550 and standard method SM 5520F [17] and analyzed by Fourier transform IR spectroscopy (FTIR) at Envirochem, Mobile, AL. 2.5 Application of the oil In June and November, ten cores (9.5 cm id, 24 cm height) were collected from subtidal bare sediments to a depth of ~20 cm for ![Map of the study site on Dauphin Island, AL, USA.](page_101_1342_1342_670.png) Figure 1. Map of the study site on Dauphin Island, AL, USA. determination of sediment oxygen consumption (SOD), nutrient fluxes, and denitrification rates. In addition, six cores for measuring rates of potential denitrification and nitrogen fixation were collected. All cores were brought back to the laboratory and the overlying water was gently removed. Half of the cores were oiled, while the remainder served as controls. The oil was applied by injecting 0.1 mL of the oil at a depth of 5 cm in ten evenly spaced locations across the cores. After oiling, cores were inundated for 12 h by gently adding 100 mL of unfiltered site water. Overlying water was then removed and sediments were exposed to air for 12 h. This cycle of inundation and air exposure was similar to the timing of semidiurnal tides at this location and was repeated for 3 days with the same water from each core. 2.6 Potential N₂ fixation and denitrification The top 5 cm from triplicate oiled and control cores were homogenized following the application of the oil and a 3-day inundation/exposure period and used for rate measurements. Nitrogen fixation rates were determined with the acetylene reduction technique [18]. Approximately 20 g of sediment from each core was measured into 70 mL serum vials and mixed with 40 mL GF/F filtered site water. Samples were sealed with butyl rubber stoppers, flushed with N₂ gas for 10 min and injected with 7 mL acetylene. Vials were incubated in the dark for 24 h, and then thoroughly shaken, before the headspace concentration of ethylene (C₂H₄) was determined on a Shimadzu gas chromatograph equipped with a flame ionization detector. Bunsen gas solubility coefficients for ethylene for the appropriate salinity and temperature were used to calculate the total amount of ethylene produced [19]. Production rates of ethylene were converted to N₂ fixation rates with a 3:1 ethylene to N₂ reduction ratio [18]. Rates of potential denitrification were determined with the acetylene inhibition technique [20] as previously described [21]. Briefly, 20 g of sediment from each core was measured into 70 mL serum vials and mixed with 35 mL GF/F filtered site water. Samples were amended with nitrate to a final concentration of 100 μM, sealed with butyl rubber stoppers and flushed with nitrogen gas for 10 min. 7 mL of acetylene was injected into each vial and incubated for 1 h. Vials were shaken vigorously prior to sampling the headspace. Headspace N₂O concentrations were measured on a gas chromatograph, Shimadzu 2014, equipped with an electron capture detector and used to calculate potential denitrification rates. The nitrous oxide solubility coefficients [22] were used to calculate total nitrous oxide produced (headspace and dissolved). Potential denitrification as well nitrogen fixation rates were converted from a gram basis to an areal basis. 2.7 Experimental setup for benthic flux measurements Five oiled and five control cores were placed underwater in an environmental chamber set to the average water temperature and allowed to equilibrate for 3 days with aerobic overlying water to ensure that no bubbles would be formed when the cores were capped. Incubations were carried out in the dark to prevent interference by photosynthetic algae [23] or bubble formation. Cores were capped underwater ensuring no air bubbles were formed and each core was equipped with a magnetic stir bar to mix the overlying water. GF/F filtered site water, enriched to a final concentration of 50 μM of isotopically labeled sodium nitrate (Na⁺¹⁵NO₃⁻), was then flowed through each core at a rate of ~2.5 mL min⁻¹. The positive displacement of the overlying water exited the core through an outflow tube ("outflow") and was collected in a reservoir. After 24 h of flow through, water samples were collected from the outflow and inflow from each core for determination of oxygen, nutrients and nitrogen gas isotope concentrations (described below). Following the sample collections, the cores were gently uncapped and the top 5 cm from each was sectioned and homogenized for THP analysis. 2.8 Benthic fluxes Sediment oxygen demand was determined from inflow and outflow water based on O₂ concentrations measured with a Unisense® multimeter equipped with a calibrated O₂ (Ox-500) sensor. Water samples were collected in triplicate from the inflow and outflow lines, filtered through GF/F and immediately frozen until analysis for inorganic nutrient concentrations as previously described. Inflow and outflow samples from each core were collected in triplicate in 12 mL Exetainers® by overflowing the vial's volume twice for the analysis of isotopes of nitrogen gas with membrane inlet MS (MIMS), equipped with an in-line quartz column packed with copper turnings and heated to 600°C [24], to remove oxygen upstream of the mass spectrometer. Samples were then preserved with 250 μL of 50% w/v ZnCl₂, capped and stored underwater until analysis within 48 h. Denitrification was determined according to the isotope pairing technique (IPT) as described in [25]. In this approach, denitrification is explicitly calculated from the \(^{29}\mathrm{N}_2\) and \(^{30}\mathrm{N}_2\) fluxes calculated from dissolved \(^{29}\mathrm{N}_2/^{28}\mathrm{N}_2\) and \(^{30}\mathrm{N}_2/^{28}\mathrm{N}_2\) measured with the MIMS. Denitrification of \(^{15}\mathrm{NO}_3^-\) (\(D_{15}\)) was calculated directly: \[ D_{15} = F^{29} + 2F^{30} \] where \(F^{29}\) and \(F^{30}\) represent the steady state \(^{29}\mathrm{N}_2\) and \(^{30}\mathrm{N}_2\) fluxes. Denitrification of \(^{14}\mathrm{NO}_3^-\) (\(D_{14}\)) was calculated using the expression of Nielsen [25]: \[ D_{14} = \frac{F^{29}}{2F^{30}} D_{15} \] Total denitrification was then calculated as the sum of \(D_{14}\) and \(D_{15}\), and hereafter referred to as "denitrification capacity." Benthic fluxes were calculated according to: \[ F = (C_e - .C_i)V/A \] where \(C_e\) is the outflow concentration, \(C_i\) is the inflow concentration, V is the flow rate, and A is the surface area of the sediment. 2.9 Anaerobic ammonium oxidation (anammox) Anammox slurries were created in duplicate 1 L bottles of artificial seawater at the same salinity as the site water and autoclaved for 1 h. Once cooled, homogenized surface sediments from 0 to 5 cm depth were added for the control and the oil treatment cores, and the slurry was continuously stirred for 1 h while being purged with N₂ gas. Slurries were then amended with Na¹⁵NO₃ to a final concentration of 50 μM. The contents of the slurry were then dispensed into 12 mL Exetainers® and incubated at in situ temperature. Triplicate samples for each treatment were preserved with 250 μL of 50% w/v ZnCl₂ over six time points over a 48-h period, analyzed on the MIMS, with anammox rates calculated from the equations of Thamdrup and Dalsgaard [26]. 2.10 Statistical analysis Two-way ANOVA was used to test the seasonal and treatment effects across the study sites for denitrification and nutrient fluxes, chlorophyll content, extractable nutrients, and potential denitrification and nitrogen fixation rates. ANOVA was run with R-software routine. When necessary, data were log10 transformed to meet the homoscedasticity assumption. 3 Results 3.1 Nitrogen fixation, potential denitrification, and anammox Despite higher TPH concentrations in the oil treatment (Fig. 2) as well as differing salinity, temperatures, sediment chl-α concentrations, water column and pore water nutrient concentrations (Table 1, Fig. 3), nitrogen fixation and potential denitrification did not differ between the treatments (Table 2). The contribution of anammox to N₂ production was <4% during the sampling date in both treatments (Table 2). Nitrogen fixation averaged 1.79 ± 0.44 and 3.03 ± 0.80 μmol N m⁻² h⁻¹ in June and November, respectively, and was lower than potential denitrification by orders of magnitude (average 959 ± 49 and 782 ± 45 μmol N m⁻² h⁻¹ in June and November, respectively) (Table 2). The range of variability in the water column nutrients was overshadowed by those in the sediments where sediment ammonium concentrations, for example, varied by as much as 200 nmol g⁻¹ dry sediment. 3.2 Benthic fluxes SOD and inorganic nutrient fluxes did not differ between the oil and control treatments (Table 2). However, consistent with warmer temperatures in June, SOD was 48% higher compared to rates measured in November (Table 2). Inorganic nutrient fluxes were also temporally variable, with more than two times higher sediment nitrate uptake and more than three times higher ammonium efflux in June than in November (Table 2). Sediments were a phosphorus source to the water column in June, but this pattern was reversed in November. Similar to SOD and inorganic nitrogen fluxes, denitrification in June exceeded rates in November (Table 2). Denitrification capacity increased with increasing SOD with a greater slope in June (0.085, \( r^2 = 0.43, \ p = 0.037 \)) than in November (0.016, \( r^2 = 0.44, \ p = 0.034 \)) (Fig. 4a). Denitrification capacity also increased with greater sediment nitrate uptake but with a more constrained range of variability in November compared to June (Fig. 4b) and rates did not differ between the treatments (Table 2).

For examples, chl-a inventories, which are an indicator of the abundance of microphytobenthos and are often used as a proxy for labile organic matter in the sediments, were similar to prior measurements in this region, which generally range from 20 to 150 mg m⁻² [21, 27, 28]. Sediment oxygen consumption and nutrient fluxes were within the range of fluxes measured in other temperate and tropical estuaries [27–29] in both oiled and control sediments. Sediment TPH concentrations measured in coastal Alabama in the aftermath of the Deepwater Horizon spill reached concentrations of 200 mg kg⁻¹. The oil additions to the study cores increased TPH concentrations to levels much greater than those measured in Alabama marshes affected by the DWH spill [30, 31]. Despite this increase, nitrogen fixation and denitrification were unaffected. The rates of denitrification capacity measured with the IPT were on the lower range of values measured with the same technique [32, 33] and significantly exceeded anammox. The minor contribution of anammox to N₂ production is consistent with other studies, suggesting that anammox does not appear to be a significant pathway for nitrogen loss in estuarine environments [21, 34, 35] that could be affected by oil contamination. Rates of potential denitrification, when nitrate concentrations were elevated compared to in situ pore water concentrations, increased substantially compared to rates measured with IPT. This higher rate of denitrification when nitrate is abundant, suggests the presence of an extant microbial community capable of responding to increased nitrate availability. Interestingly, the presence of oil did not affect the magnitude of the increase in denitrification in response to higher nitrate availability. This extant microbial community carrying out denitrification can greatly contribute to nitrogen removal in the sediments and potentially limit the Figure 3. Concentrations of total extractable pore water ammonium, nitrate + nitrite, and phosphate in the surficial sediments (\( n = 3 \) for each depth, average \( \pm \) standard error). availability of nitrogen to hydrocarbon degrading microorganisms, which are often nitrogen limited [36]. Gilbert et al. [37] were able to experimentally link oxygen availability and potential denitrification in coastal sediments after exposure to hydrocarbons. The authors initially measured a reduction (83%) of potential denitrification in contaminated sediments, with a gradual increase over time. The sharp decline was attributed to lower oxygen availability and the increase in denitrification with time was attributed to the bioturbating fauna that (i) increased the oxygen supply, which could enhance coupled nitrification–denitrification within the sediments at the oxic anoxic microzones; and (ii) the supply of nitrate from the water column to deeper regions within the sediments where denitrification could occur. This observation of a higher slope for denitrification capacity versus SOD in the summer compared to the fall is also indicative of a tighter coupling of nitrification-denitrification in June than in November, and furthermore suggests that oil spills at concentrations that negatively impact the nitrifiers [38] or sediment oxygen availability, which is required for nitrification, will have a larger effect in the summer than in the winter months on denitrification. In a previous investigation with sediments from a nearby marsh exposed to high hydrocarbon loads (4000 mg kg\(^{-1}\)), nitrogen fixation was enhanced [31], but interestingly, at oil additions of 500 mg kg\(^{-1}\) nitrogen fixation rates were unaffected. In mesocosm experiments, Horel et al. [31] also reported that potential denitrification rates in marsh sediments exposed to hydrocarbons were higher than controls with sediments incubated at 10 and 30°C, with the highest potential denitrification measured in sediments contaminated with highly weathered crude oil at 4000 mg kg\(^{-1}\). However, similar to results for nitrogen fixation, rates of denitrification in sediments contaminated at lower levels (500 mg kg\(^{-1}\)) and at concentrations similar to the current study were not affected. Others have also noted a threshold of contamination affecting nitrogen cycling. Schafer et al. [39] exposed sediments from the sub-Antarctic region to a range of oil concentrations (0–50–000 mg kg\(^{-1}\)), and found that while denitrification potentials were unaffected, nitrification was inhibited at hydrocarbon concentrations exceeding 190 mg kg\(^{-1}\). The impacts of oil on nitrogen cycling in marine sediments have been variable with several studies reporting declines in denitrification [7, 8], while other have shown increased denitrification [9, 10], or still no changes in rates of denitrification in oiled sediments [6]. Several of the studies that show minor effects of crude oil contamination on processes in the nitrogen cycle are from regions that have been previously exposed to crude oil. For example, Bonin et al. [7] showed that changes in potential denitrification at six sites on the Mediterranean coast following exposure to oil at a concentration of 10 g kg\(^{-1}\) of sediment varied depending on the sites. While rates of denitrification declined at five of the sites, rates remained high and invariant at the site located near a refinery that had been a chronic source of hydrocarbon contamination. Deni and Penninckx [40] also reported that nitrification was not affected by additional oil inputs in sediments collected from areas previously exposed to hydrocarbon and attributed this finding to a higher affinity for ammonium by microbes at the contaminated sites. In our study region, Horel et al. [41] measured moderately high background hydrocarbon degrader microorganisms, as well as a large temporal variability in abundances of hydroclastic microorganisms in the sediments. Horel et al. [41] suggested that these findings were consistent with prior exposure to hydrocarbons caused by accidental marine fuel from the naval traffic at this location, as well as an active microbial community that is predisposed to oil contamination. The resiliency in nitrogen cycling to further contamination at our site is, therefore, consistent with prior results that show minor changes in rates Table 2. Current remediation strategies of oiled ecosystems include application of nitrogen, or nitrogen and phosphorus fertilizers to oiled sediments [12, 13]. Increasing the supply of inorganic nutrients to sediments lowers the nutrient limitation of the hydrocarbonoclastic microbial community and leads to enhanced rates of hydrocarbon degradation. Optimizing the concentrations of pore water inorganic nutrients by application of fertilizers that result in the greatest hydrocarbon degradation, however, remains challenging [14, 42]. This data suggests that while additional input of oil at a site with a prior history of contamination does not lead to increased denitrification; however, denitrification increases substantially in response to higher nitrate availability. Therefore, if the remediation of a chronically oiled site relies on the application of fertilizers, monitoring pore water nitrate availability will be necessary to ensure that concentrations are maintained at levels that are adequate for optimal hydrocarbon degradation. Significant nonsymbiotic nitrogen fixation in Patagonian ombrotrophic bogs

KLAUS-HOLGER KNORR1, MARCUS A. HORN2 and WERNER BORKEN3
1Institute for Landscape Ecology, Hydrology Group, University of Münster, Heisenbergstr. 2, 48149 Münster, Germany,
2Department of Ecological Microbiology, University of Bayreuth, Dr.-Hans-Frisch-Str. 1-3, 95448 Bayreuth, Germany,
3Department of Soil Ecology, University of Bayreuth, Dr.-Hans-Frisch-Str. 1-3, 95448 Bayreuth, Germany

Abstract

Nitrogen (N) nutrition in pristine peatlands relies on the natural input of inorganic N through atmospheric deposition or biological dinitrogen (N2) fixation. However, N2 fixation and its significance for N cycling, plant productivity, and peat buildup are mostly associated with the presence of Sphagnum mosses. Here, we report high nonsymbiotic N2-fixation rates in two pristine Patagonian bogs with diversified vegetation and natural N deposition. Nonsymbiotic N2 fixation was measured in samples from 0 to 10, 10 to 20, and 40 to 50 cm depth using the 15N2 assay as well as the acetylene reduction assay (ARA). The ARA considerably underestimated N2 fixation and can thus not be recommended for peatland studies. Based on the 15N2 assay, high nonsymbiotic N2-fixation rates of 0.3–1.4 μmol N2 g−1 day−1 were found down to 50 cm under micro-oxic conditions (2 vol.%) in samples from plots covered by Sphagnum magellanicum or by vascular cushion plants, latter characterized by dense and deep aerenchyma roots. Peat N concentrations point to greater potential of nonsymbiotic N2 fixation under cushion plants, likely because of the availability of easily decomposable organic compounds and oxic conditions in the rhizosphere. In the Sphagnum plots, high N2 fixation below 10 cm depth rather reflects the potential during dry periods or low water level when oxygen penetrates the top peat layer and triggers peat mineralization. Natural abundance of the 15N isotope of live Sphagnum (5.6 δ‰) from 0 to 10 cm points to solely N uptake from atmospheric deposition and nonsymbiotic N2 fixation. A mean 15N signature of −0.7 δ‰ of peat from the cushion plant plots indicates additional N supply from N mineralization. Our findings suggest that nonsymbiotic N2 fixation overcomes N deficiency in different vegetation communities and has great significance for N cycling and peat accumulation in pristine peatlands.

Introduction

Peatlands store approximately 30% of the global soil organic carbon (C) mainly accumulated and preserved during the Holocene in the past 11 700 years (Gorham, 1991). Plant growth and peat accumulation rely on the permanent input of reactive nitrogen (N) as the recycling of organic N by mineralization is restricted by anoxic conditions in waterlogged peatlands. Natural N input by means of lightning of about 0.1 g m−2 yr−1 is an essential source of reactive N (Bragazza et al., 2005), but net accumulation rates of 0.2–0.5 g N m−2 yr−1 point to additional N sources (Loisel et al., 2014). Biological fixation of molecular nitrogen (N2) by symbiotic, associative, and free-living bacteria and archaea (diazotrophic organisms) is a widespread process that improves the N supply in N-limited ecosystems (Vitousek et al., 2013). It is generally thought that the potential of symbiotic N2 fixation is much greater than of associative and nonsymbiotic N2 fixation because of the high energy cost for enzymatic reduction of N2 to ammonia (NH3).

Indeed, peatlands inhabit only few plant species such as Myrica gale that host symbiotic N2-fixing bacteria in root nodules (Schwintzer, 1979). However, these symbiotic N2-fixing plant species do not exist in all peatlands or grow only in ecological niches. There are other non-nodule-forming plants which are associated with different groups of N2-fixing bacteria. N2-fixing heterocystous cyanobacteria are associated with Sphagnum mosses and increase the productivity of Sphagnum by higher N supply (Basilier et al., 1978). Recent studies indicate high N2 fixation by methanotrophic bacteria/archaea in or on the tissues of Sphagnum mosses (Bragina et al., 2013; Larmola et al., 2014). The N2-fixation rate is linked to oxidation of methane (CH4) as the main energy source (Larmola et al., 2014). From other ecosystems, it is known that different N2-fixing bacteria species live in the rhizosphere, as endophytes in intercellular spaces within live plant tissues or in intracellular spaces of dead plant cells (Franché et al., 2009). Despite their frequent appearance, N2 fixation seems to

</page>

<page number="1">

vary among peatland types. Minerotrophic fens have much greater N₂-fixation rates than ombrotrophic bogs (Waughman & Bellamy, 1980). Because of effective associations between diazotrophs and living parts of mosses, most studies focused on N₂-fixing activity in the top peat layer and did not consider the activity in underlying bare peat. However, given the large peat mass, even small N₂-fixing rates in subsurface peat could be relevant for the N cycle.

Patagonian peatlands differ from peatlands of the northern hemisphere by their plant diversity. Two vascular cushion plants, Astelia pumila and Donatia fascicularis, characterized by high density and biomass of aerenchyma roots in the top peat layer, dominate large areas in Patagonian bogs (Kleinebecker et al., 2010). Aerenchyma roots strongly increase the gas exchange between peat and the atmosphere, enabling enhanced mineralization of organic matter, and efficient CH₄ oxidation in the rhizosphere (Fritz et al., 2011). Elevated oxygen (O₂) concentrations in the rhizosphere and considerable amounts of easily decomposable organic compounds by root exudation and root litter could provide energy sources for heterotrophic free-living diazotrophs (Dobbelaere et al., 2003). The vertical extent of aerenchyma roots generates favorable conditions for diazotrophs even in subsurface peat layers under cushion plants. Thus, N₂ fixation activity could be higher in A. pumila and D. fascicularis dominated patches than in Sphagnum dominated patches.

Natural abundance of the \(^{15}\)N isotope in plant tissues or plant detritus gives insight into the N sources used for growth (Högberg, 1997). Organic N originating from symbiotic and associative diazotrophs has typically a \(^{15}\)N signature close to zero like atmospheric N₂ (Stewart et al., 2011). Fractionation processes via N mineralization of organic matter by fungi and subsequent transfer to the plant leads to \(^{15}\)N depletion in plant tissues and \(^{15}\)N enrichment in fungal hyphae (Hobbie & Högberg, 2012).

Biological N₂ fixation is often assessed by the acetylene reduction assay (ARA) or the uptake of \(^{15}\)N₂ in incubation chambers (Weaver & Danso, 1994). ARA is sensitive and easy to measure by ethylene (C₂H₄) production but needs calibration by \(^{15}\)N₂ uptake due to the variable molar C₂H₄ : \(^{15}\)N₂ conversion ratio. The application of ARA in peatland studies could be critical because acetylene inhibits the enzyme methane mono-oxygenase and thereby the N₂ fixation of methanotrophs (Flett et al., 1975). N₂-fixation rates in peatlands might thus be underestimated as ARA was often used without \(^{15}\)N₂ calibration.

Here, we assess the nonsymbiotic N₂ fixation in plots dominated either by Sphagnum or by cushion plants of two bogs in South Patagonia using ARA and the \(^{15}\)N₂ method. We hypothesize that (1) the N₂-fixing rate is greater under cushion plants with high density and biomass of aerenchyma roots than under Sphagnum, (2) the N₂-fixation rate decreases with depth, and (3) the natural \(^{15}\)N signature in the top peat layer is linked to the observed N₂-fixation rate.

Material and methods

Site description

Samples were taken from two pristine ombrotrophic bogs in Southern Patagonia, Chile, in March 2014. Both bogs are acidic with pH values between 4 and 5 in the top peat layer. The bog SKY has an area of about 8 km² and is located at the coast of the Seno Skyring (eastern access –52.508667°S, 72.127278°W). Peat thickness ranges between 3 and 4 m and the oldest peat has an age of about 11 000 years. An ash layer from the eruption of the volcano Mount Burney 4444 BP (Kilian & Lamy, 2012) was found in 100–275 cm depth. Sediment layers and differences in peat quality indicated several changes in vegetation with periods of woody shrubs, vascular plants, and Sphagnum mosses.

The bog OBS (–52.135907°S, 72.446037°W) has an area of 0.3 km², a few meter above the sea level, and is located close the Seno Obstrucción, south of the town Puerto Natales. Peat thickness is 2–3 m and the ash layer of the Mount Burney eruption was not present at this site, indicating that this bog developed after 4444 BP.

The climate of southwest Patagonia is characterized by cool temperatures, strong gradients in precipitation, and strong western wind. Annual precipitation in the eastern slopes of the southern Andes is about 1000 mm and increases to 6000–7000 mm along the south Patagonian west coast (Schneider et al., 2003). At the Seno Skyring, mean annual precipitation is about 1500 mm, mean annual air temperature is about 6.4 °C with minimum monthly temperatures of about 2 °C in June/July and maximum temperatures of 10–11 °C from December to February. Climate parameters were not measured at OBS, but climate is similar to SKY because of its geographical location.

Present vegetation of both bogs is dominated by Sphagnum magellanicum, A. pumila, D. fascicularis, Lepidothamnus fonkii, Tetracium magellanicum, Oreobolus obtusangulus, Caltha appendiculata, Empetrum rubrum, Gaultheria pumila, Drosera uniflora, Marsippospermum grandiflorum, Polytrichum spec., Carex magellonica. The vascular plant species A. pumila and D. fascicularis have large aerenchyma root biomass in the top peat layer with single roots down to 120 cm depth (Fritz et al., 2011).

Sampling

We sampled six cores using a Russian peat corer (inner diameter 5 cm) from 0 to 50 cm depth at each of the two plots at both sites. The Sphagnum plots (SKY-SPH, OBS-SPH) were water saturated (i.e., 0–1 cm below the surface of Sphagnum capitula) while the plots with cushion plants (SKY-CP, OBS-CP), including A. pumila and D. fascicularis,

</page>

<page number="2">

had water levels 3–5 centimeters below the surface. Cores were separated into 0–10, 10–20, and 40–50 cm sections and stored in whirl packs at 4 °C until further processing. Green biomass and live roots of samples from SKY-CP and OBS-CP were completely removed for determination of N₂ fixation. Samples from SKY-SPH and OBS-SPH consisted of live (0–10 cm), partly dead (10–20 cm), or dead plant residues of S. magellanicum.

Sphagnum density (g d.w. cm⁻³) was determined by taking cores of 100 cm² from 0 to 20 cm depth (n = 3). Peat density (g d.w. cm⁻³) at 0–10, 10–20, and 40–50 cm depth was determined using a Russian corer as above (n = 3). Peat density at 0–10 and 10–20 cm depth in the CP plots was corrected by aerenchyma root biomass. Root biomass in the CP plots was determined by picking live roots from additional 100 cm² cores down 20 cm depth. All samples were air-dried at 40 °C. Total phosphorus (P) contents of one mixed sample per plot and depth were analyzed by wavelength-dispersive X-ray fluorescence spectroscopy (WD-XRF), using a Rigaku Primus ZSX II (Rigaku, Tokyo, Japan), calibrated with certified reference materials.

Nitrogen fixation

Nitrogen fixation was determined by two different methods as described by Weaver & Danso (1994): incubation of samples with \(^{15}\mathrm{N}_2\) and the ARA. Latter consists of the reduction of acetylene (C₂H₂) to ethylene (C₂H₄) by diazotrophic organisms. The amount of produced C₂H₄ is related to the N₂-fixation rate, but the molar C₂H₄:N₂ ratio is variable depending on plant species, soil, and environmental conditions. Incubation of samples with \(^{15}\mathrm{N}_2\) and subsequent analysis of \(^{15}\mathrm{N}\) excess in plant or soil are generally used for calibration of ARA. For parallel application of both methods, glass vials of 22 mL volume were filled with 2–3 g (fresh weight) of S. magellanicum or peat/plant detritus, closed with stoppers and crimp seals. Immediately after closure, glass vials were flushed with pure N₂ gas (natural \(^{15}\mathrm{N}\) abundance) for 1 min at a flux rate of 200 mL per minute. An oxygen (O₂) concentration of about 2 vol. % was adjusted in each vial by injection of 0.5 mL pure O₂ for both the \(^{15}\mathrm{N}_2\) and ARA application.

The \(^{15}\mathrm{N}_2\) incubation was initiated by injection of 8 mL \(^{15}\mathrm{N}_2\) (98 atom %, Sigma-Aldrich), resulting in 30–35 atom% \(^{15}\mathrm{N}_2\) in the headspace. The \(^{15}\mathrm{N}_2\) concentration of each vial was calculated by pressure measurements using a digital pressure meter (GMH 3111; GHM Messtechnik GmbH, Regenstauf, Germany) with an accuracy of 1 mbar before and after \(^{15}\mathrm{N}_2\) injection. Additionally, the \(^{15}\mathrm{N}_2\) concentration was measured for a set of 20 samples by the Centre of Stable Isotopes Research and Analysis at the University of Göttingen, Germany. For this purpose, the uneven distribution of \(^{15}\mathrm{N}\) and \(^{14}\mathrm{N}\) in N₂ of the gas samples, mainly existing of the mass 28 and 30, was equilibrated using a microwave (Modell GMW 24-201, AHF Analysentechnik, Tübingen, Germany) (Well et al., 1998). Afterward, the \(^{15}\mathrm{N}\) abundance was measured with mass spectrometer (Thermo Finnigan Delta plus XL, Thermo Fisher Scientific Inc., Waltham, MA, USA). The deviation among pressure measurements and \(^{15}\mathrm{N}_2\) analysis was <2 atom%.

The \(^{15}\mathrm{N}_2\) incubation lasted 72–80 h and took place in a climate chamber at 15 °C in the dark. Afterward, vials were opened and peat samples were immediately freeze-dried. The \(^{15}\mathrm{N}\) abundance as well as total C and N contents of all nonincubated and \(^{15}\mathrm{N}_2\) incubated samples was measured using an elemental analyzer (EA 3000, HekaTech, Wegberg, Germany) coupled to a isotope ratio mass spectrometer (NU instruments, Wrexham, UK), calibrated with IAEA standards. The accuracy of \(^{15}\mathrm{N}\) analysis determined by repeated analysis was 0.1 \(δ^{15}\mathrm{N}\). After conversion of the \(δ^{15}\mathrm{N}\) notation into atom% \(^{15}\mathrm{N}\), the \(^{15}\mathrm{N}\) enrichment factor (E) in an incubated sample (peat labeled) was calculated in relation to the \(^{15}\mathrm{N}_2\) concentration in the headspace (gas labeled) and by subtraction of the natural \(^{15}\mathrm{N}\) abundance of the corresponding unlabeled sample (peat unlabeled) and headspace (gas unlabeled) as follows:

\[
E = \frac{\text{Atom}\%^{15}\mathrm{N}_{\text{peat labeled}} - \text{Atom}\%^{15}\mathrm{N}_{\text{peat unlabeled}}}{\text{Atom}\%^{15}\mathrm{N}_{\text{gas labeled}} - \text{Atom}\%^{15}\mathrm{N}_{\text{gas unlabeled}}}
\]

The N₂-fixation rate (N₂fix) in μmol N g d.w.⁻¹ day⁻¹ was calculated as follows:

\[
\mathrm{N}_{2\text{fix}} = \frac{\mathrm{N}_{\text{peat labeled}}}{t \times m} \times E,
\]

where \(N_{\text{peat labeled}}\) is the total N content of the labeled sample (μmol), t is the incubation time (day), and m is the dry weight of the sample in the incubation vial (g).

For the ARA, an acetylene concentration of approximately 10 vol. % was adjusted in the headspace of the vials by injection of 2.5 mL pure acetylene. Additionally, three vials (blanks) were filled with 3 mL of deionized water, and the same O₂ and C₂H₂ concentration was adjusted in the headspace as described above. Glass vials had an initial overpressure of 100–150 mbar. Samples were incubated for 28 h at 15 °C in the dark. Ethylene concentration was analyzed at 0, 6, 22, and 28 h using a gas chromatograph (Model 8610C, SRI Instruments Inc., Las Vegas, NV, USA) equipped with a Porapak T column and a flame ionization detector (FID). A gas sample was taken from the vial headspace using a 500-μL syringe, and a gas volume of 200 μL was directly injected into the gas chromatograph. Linear calibration curves were obtained from measurements of different ethylene standards. After incubation, samples were freeze-dried for determination of dry weight and further analyses. Ethylene production rates (μmol C₂H₄ g d.w.⁻¹ day⁻¹) were calculated from the linear increase in C₂H₄ concentration per day and the ideal gas law, considering air pressure and temperature in the vials.

Methane and carbon dioxide profile

In situ dissolved methane (CH₄) and carbon dioxide (CO₂) concentration profiles in the peat were determined at SKY-SPH and SKY-CP during one occasion. For this purpose, a gas diffusive equilibration sampling technique was installed consisting of a PVC pipe with 2 m of coiled silicon tubing at each sampling depth (Knorr et al., 2009). The gas phase within the silicon tubing equilibrates with the gases in pore water by diffusion within 1–2 days (Kammann et al., 2001). It reached a depth of 3.30 m with a sampling resolution of 20 cm (0–180 cm depth) and 30 cm (210–330 cm depth). A volume of

</page>

<page number="3">

3.5 mL was transferred from the silicon tubing into a 7-mL air-tight crimp vial, previously flushed with pure N₂. Concentrations of CO₂ and CH₄ were measured using a gas chromatograph (SRI 8610, SRI Instruments, Torrance, CA, USA) with methanizer and FID. Pore water concentration of dissolved inorganic carbon (DIC = CO₂ + H₂CO₃ + HCO₃⁻) and CH₄ was recalculated from gas samples of the diffusive equilibration sampler and applying Henry’s law. All constants were corrected to in situ temperature of 6 °C according to Lide & Frederikse (1995).

Statistics

Statistical analyses were performed using SYSTAT software (Systat Software, Inc., San Jose, CA, USA). The effects of site and vegetation on N₂ fixation (¹⁵N₂, ARA) were separately tested by one-way analyses of variance (ANOVA) for each depth. All data hereto were tested for normality using the Shapiro–Wilk test and if necessary were ln-transformed to match the criteria for normality.

Results

Variability in N content, N stocks, ¹⁵N signature, and C/N ratio

N contents and N stocks generally increased with depth at both study sites (Table 1). Significant differences between the sites only occurred at 10–20 cm depth with higher N contents at SKY than at OBS (P = 0.01). CP plots had significantly higher N contents than the SPH plots at 0–10 cm (P < 0.001) and 10–20 cm depth (P = 0.018) while there was no vegetation effect at 40–50 cm depth. Interpolating the N stocks for the 20–40 cm peat layer resulted into total N stocks for the top 50 cm peat layer of 190–300 g m⁻². CP plots had 32% (OBS) and 59% (SKY) higher N stocks than the SPH plots.

The molar C/N ratios ranged between 36 and 175 in the top 50 cm peat layer across both sites (Table 1). C/N ratios in the top 20 cm were smaller in the CP plots than in the SPH plots, but the differences at 40–50 cm were small between the vegetation types. Site had no effect on total P concentrations varying between 178 and 476 mg kg⁻¹ at the three depths. P concentrations decreased in the SPH plots and increased in the CP plots with depth.

The δ¹⁵N signature increased with depth from −0.7 to 3.5‰ in the CP plots (Fig. 1). Opposite pattern revealed the SPH plots with a decrease from 6.4‰ at 0–10 cm to 1.4‰ at 40–50 cm depth. Vegetation had a significant effect on the ¹⁵N signature at 0–10 cm (P < 0.001) and 40–50 cm depth (P < 0.001). There was no site effect on the pattern of the ¹⁵N signature.

Variability of N₂ fixation: ¹⁵N₂ method

N₂ fixation ranged between 0.3 and 1.4 μmol N₂ g⁻¹ day⁻¹ without clear vertical pattern, except SKY-CP exhibiting declining rates with increasing depth (Fig. 2). There was a significant site effect (OBS > SKY) on N₂ fixation at 10–20 cm (P < 0.001) and 40–50 cm (P < 0.001) depth and a significant vegetation effect (SPH > CP) for all depths (P < 0.003). The significant interaction (P = 0.004) of site and vegetation at 40–50 cm depth indicates that the site effect on N₂ fixation was different for SPH and CP.

Results from ¹⁵N₂ incubations at 15 °C were extrapolated to the field scale using peat densities of each depth. N₂-fixation rates varied from 27 to 216 mg N m⁻² day⁻¹ across both sites and all depths (Table 2). The rates were generally highest at 40–50 cm depth due to the greater peat density (0.06 g d.w. cm⁻³) compared to 0–10 and 10–20 cm depth (0.02–0.03 g d.w. cm⁻³).

Comparison of ARA and \( ^{15}\mathrm{N}_2 \)

Ethylene production varied between 0.2 and 1.3 \( \mu\mathrm{mol} \ \mathrm{g}^{-1} \ \mathrm{d.w.} \ \mathrm{day}^{-1} \) (Fig. 3). Except for the SPH plot at OBS, ethylene production strongly decreased from 0–10 to 40–50 cm. Site had no effect on ethylene production at 0–10 and 10–20 cm depth, but the rate at 40–50 cm was significantly greater in OBS than in SKY (\( P < 0.001 \)). Vegetation had significant effects on ethylene production at 0–10 cm (\( P = 0.006 \)) and 10–20 cm (\( P = 0.004 \)) depth with higher rates in the CP plots than in the SPH plots. ANOVA revealed no interactions between the two factors site and vegetation.

The mean ratio of ethylene production to \( ^{15}\mathrm{N}_2 \) uptake covered a wide span, ranging from 0.4 to 1.8 (Fig. 4). Ratios were smallest in the SPH plots, indicating a systematic vegetation effect on the ratio at 0–10 and 10–20 cm depth. In both vegetation types, the ratio decreased with increasing depth; whereby, the decline was stronger in the CP plots than in the SPH plots. At 40–50 cm depth, both vegetation types had similar ratios.

Peat profile CH<sub>4</sub> and DIC concentrations

CH<sub>4</sub> and DIC concentrations and vertical patterns differed between the SPH and CP plots at SKY (Fig. 5). In the SPH plot, CH<sub>4</sub> linearly increased from almost atmospheric concentration at 0 cm depth to a maximum of about 160 \( \mu\mathrm{mol} \ \mathrm{L}^{-1} \) at 120 cm depth. In the CP plot, CH<sub>4</sub> concentration was close to atmospheric concentration down to 100 cm depth, indicating the influence of aerenchymatic oxygen supply on CH<sub>4</sub> turnover. Single aerenchymatic roots of A. pumila were found in peat cores from 50 to 100 cm depth although their influence on oxygenation and CH<sub>4</sub> concentration at this depth is unclear. The effect of cushion plants on DIC concentrations was small. While DIC continuously increased with depth at the SPH plot, the maximum was reached in 80 cm depth at the CP plot.

Discussion

Nonsymbiotic \( \mathrm{N}_2 \) fixation in pristine peatlands

Our results demonstrate the potential of nonsymbiotic \( \mathrm{N}_2 \) fixation in two ombrotrophic bogs of Patagonia. Together with recent findings from the northern hemisphere, it changes the prevailing view of insignificant nonsymbiotic \( \mathrm{N}_2 \) fixation and N deficiency in pristine peatlands. Fig. 4 Mean (± SD) ratio of ethylene production to N₂-fixation in Sphagnum (SPH) and peat under cushion plants (CP) at three depths (n = 12). Samples from the OBS and SKY sites.

mosses fix 0.1–2.9 g N m⁻² yr⁻¹ in fens and fen–bog transitions with distinct nutrient status (Larmola et al., 2014). Likewise, a broader range of 0.5–6.2 g N m⁻² yr⁻¹ was attributed to CH₄-oxidizing bacteria in different Sphagnum species of boreal bogs (Vile et al., 2014). Basilier et al. (1978) already reported N₂-fixation rates of 0.5–6.4 g N m⁻² yr⁻¹ in the mire through an association of cyanobacteria with Sphagnum and Drepanocladus. In contrast, most of the earlier studies found rather small nonsymbiotic N₂-fixation rates in the range of <0.1–2.1 g N m⁻² yr⁻¹ (Waughman & Bellamy, 1980; Chapman & Hemond, 1982; Schwintzer, 1983). Our estimates of 63–78 mg N m⁻² day⁻¹ for the top 10 cm in living Sphagnum and peat under vascular plants exceed the average daily rates of other studies. Vile et al. (2014), for example, incubated only the top 5 cm of Sphagnum plots. We found, however, still live tissues of S. magellanicum at 10–20 cm depth and N₂ fixation even below that depth in peat from S. magellanicum. Another reason for our estimates being at the upper end is that the incubation temperature of 15 °C is higher than the mean temperature during growing season. Further, we assume that N₂ fixation in peatland was underestimated in some studies when ARA was used as solely method without calibration by the \(^{15}\)N₂ assay (see below). Therefore, we refer here to N₂-fixation rates determined with the \(^{15}\)N₂ assay.

The potential of nonsymbiotic N₂ fixation is hardly smaller in the peat layers below 10 cm depth, although we expect much smaller rates under in situ conditions. Disturbance of peat by sampling, root picking and thereby penetration of O₂ have likely triggered a sudden rise in the activity of heterotrophic diazotrophs. The adjusted O₂ concentration of about 2% during incubation was obviously sufficient for ongoing high activity of heterotrophic microorganisms. Similar conditions should irregularly arise in situ by water table fluctuations. Nonsymbiotic N₂ fixation could thus be stimulated in transient oxic peat layers during dry periods.

Most studies exclusively report on nonsymbiotic N₂ fixation in association with Sphagnum or other mosses (c.f. Basilier et al., 1978; Larmola et al., 2014; Vile et al., 2014). Slightly lower N₂-fixation rates under cushion plants in the absence of Sphagnum point to similar N availability in both vegetation types. In fact, we assume higher in situ rates under cushion plants for different reasons. First, the enormous biomass of aerenchyma roots acts as conduit for gas exchange between peat and the atmosphere in the top 50–100 cm of the peat. Redox potentials of >350 mV to a depth of 150 cm indicate the presence of O₂ in the rhizosphere of cushion plants while O₂ is almost absent in peat under Sphagnum (Fritz et al., 2011). Although O₂ profiles were not measured at our plots, low CH₄ concentrations down to 90 cm depth at the SKY-CP plot suggest thorough CH₄ oxidation in the rhizosphere at oxic conditions. Second, the cushion plants A. pumila and D. fascicularis release root exudates and produce relatively easily decomposable, barely lignified aerenchyma roots. We determined live root biomass of 0.9–1.1 kg d.w. m⁻² and estimated mean lifetimes of about 3–4 years using radiocarbon dating (data not shown), pointing to high root turnover.

</page>

<page number="6">

Fig. 5 CH₄ and dissolved inorganic carbon (DIC) concentrations in peat pore water at different depth at (a) SKY-SPH and (b) SKY-CP.

Addition of root exudates or sugars induces a rapid increase in nonsymbiotic N₂ fixation (Bürgmann et al., 2005). An increase of N₂ fixation in two moss species also was achieved by long-term addition of birch litter (Sorensen & Michelsen, 2011), demonstrating the dependency of heterotrophic diazotrophs on C sources. Hence, the rhizosphere under cushion plants represents a favorable milieu for free-living diazotrophs.

Although the litter of Sphagnum is refractory and mainly contributes to peat accumulation (Bragazza et al., 2007), dissolved organic carbon (DOC) from Sphagnum leachates is easily biodegradable (Wickland et al., 2007). The increase in O₂ availability and consequent activation of oxygen-dependent enzymes like phenol oxidases (Freeman et al., 2004) in Sphagnum peat could have resulted into decomposition of both refractory organic compounds and DOC. Whether CH₄-oxidizing bacteria, the prevailing active diazotrophs in Sphagnum (Vile et al., 2014), or other diazotrophs were stimulated during sample processing remains unclear. Our apparent N₂-fixation rates for peat likely overestimated in situ conditions and rather demonstrate the potential of N₂ fixation at reduced water level.

Nitrogen status of ombrotrophic bogs

High apparent nonsymbiotic N₂-fixation rates suggest that N is a nonlimiting nutrient for plant growth in the studied peatlands, although N concentrations in the top 10 cm indicate small net N uptake and retention by vegetation. N fertilization did not affect biomass production, whereas the combined fertilization of N and P almost doubled biomass production of Sphagnum in a Patagonian bog (Fritz et al., 2012). Considering small P concentrations in the SPH and CP plots, P seems to be a limiting macronutrient of vegetation in the bogs, not N.

Input of inorganic N by deposition may have different implications on plant communities and plant traits than organic N input by N₂ fixation (van der Heijden et al., 2000; Malmer et al., 2003). Sphagnum mosses absorb inorganic N from deposition very efficiently on the surface through the capitula up to about 1 g N m⁻² yr⁻¹. (Nordbakken et al., 2003; Fritz et al., 2014). Vascular plants additionally take up inorganic N via their root system and thus rely on N recycling by mineralization of plant litter or nonsymbiotic N₂ fixation. The vertical profile of natural \(^{15}\)N signatures underlines the distinct N nutrition of plants in the CP and SPH plots. Negative \(δ^{15}\)N signatures in the vegetation of the CP plots indicate uptake of mineralized N and preceding discrimination of the \(^{15}\)N isotope by fungi. The \(^{15}\)N isotopes enrich at underlying peat layers, and the \(^{15}\)N signature becomes more positive. The slightly negative \(^{15}\)N signature of \(-0.7\%\%\) at 0–10 cm depth suggests that N₂ fixation also plays an important role for cushion plants. The positive \(^{15}\)N signature of \(6.7\%\%\) at 0–10 cm depth in the SPH plots provides evidence that N₂ fixation and N deposition are the dominant N sources for Sphagnum and that N mineralization is negligible. However, Sphagnum also may exhibit negative \(δ^{15}\)N signatures when mineralized N is available (Broder et al., 2012). It is difficult to assess the origin of N in plants because N deposition, N₂ fixation, and N mineralization display main potential sources with varying isotopic signature. Overall, higher N concentrations and smaller C/N ratios underpin the strength of N acquisition in the CP plots compared to the SPH plots.

Our data suggest that only a certain portion of fixed N remains in the peatlands. Net sequestration of about 1 g N m⁻² yr⁻¹ is likely, considering peat accumulation rates of 20–90 g C m⁻² yr⁻¹ in Patagonian bogs (Loisel & Yu, 2013) and C/N ratios of <50 below the

</page>

<page number="7">

rooting zone at our sites. Differences between potential N₂ fixation and N sequestration can be explained by N losses, but these need to be verified by further investigations.

Comparison of methods

Ethylene production was small compared to \(^{15}\mathrm{N}_2\) fixation resulting into overall small ratios of 0.4–1.8. Our ratios are considerably smaller than the theoretical ratio of 3 : 1 or 4 : 1 that was used for estimates of N₂ fixation in many studies (Weaver & Danso, 1994). A plausible explanation for small C₂H₄ production would be the inhibitory effect of C₂H₂ on the CH₄ monooxygenase and thus of methanotrophic bacteria which have the ability to fix molecular N₂ (Flett et al., 1975). Nitrogenase genes (i.e., nifH coding for one subunit of the Mo-dependent nitrogenase) and transcripts related to the methanotrophic genera Methylocapsa and Methyloferula were detected in peatlands (Vile et al., 2014). Highest N₂ fixation and CH₄ oxidation rates likewise co-occurred in such systems (Larmola et al., 2014). Thus, inhibition of CH₄-oxidizing diazotrophs by high acetylene concentrations leads to reduced C₂H₄ production and underestimation of nitrogen fixation in peatland soils. The observed vegetation effect, that is, the different ratios of ethylene production to \(^{15}\mathrm{N}_2\) fixation under Sphagnum and cushion plants could be possibly attributed to different communities of diazotrophs. Microbial oxidation of C₂H₄ is known for peat soils although acclimation of several days is required until significant C₂H₄ consumption is observed, suggesting only a minor impact of C₂H₄ consuming microbes on N₂ fixation by the ARA (Elsgaard, 2000).

It should be noted that the \(^{15}\mathrm{N}_2\) assay also may underestimate the true fixation rate. The \(^{15}\mathrm{N}_2\) assay assumes complete equilibration of \(^{15}\mathrm{N}_2\) between the gaseous and aqueous phase. As \(^{15}\mathrm{N}_2\) is generally injected in gaseous form and as N₂ has a small water solubility, it needs some time before it equilibrates with the aqueous phase and the \(^{15}\mathrm{N}_2\) fixation is accordingly smaller during the beginning of incubation. Therefore, the length of incubation and the amount of water or thickness of water film would affect the fixation rate. Application of \(^{15}\mathrm{N}_2\) in dissolved form vs. gaseous form doubled the N₂-fixation rate of ocean water (Großkopf et al., 2012). Implementation of this methodological advancement could even reappraise the role of nonsymbiotic N₂ fixation in peatlands.

In conclusion, nonsymbiotic N₂ fixation is an important component of the N cycle and prevents N deficiency in ombrotrophic bogs. The potential of nonsymbiotic N₂ fixation in the top 50 cm implies strong regulation by water level fluctuations and oxygen penetration. CH₄ availability could be another regulating factor when CH₄-oxidizing diazotrophs dominate nonsymbiotic N₂ fixation. N cycling and N₂ fixation seem to differ between patches covered by cushion plants and Sphagnum. Disturbance of the O₂ concentration and water status by taking peat samples has apparently strong influence on the rate of N₂ fixation. An in situ method without any disturbance is needed to ascertain the dynamics and pattern of nonsymbiotic N₂ fixation on ecosystem scale. Such a methodological progress could lead to a global re-evaluation of N₂ fixation and N cycling in peatlands. Further, similar to N₂ fixation by associations of mosses and cyanobacteria (Lindo et al., 2013), nonsymbiotic N₂ fixation could be a key driver of the C balance in peatlands.

NITROGEN ASSESSMENTS IN A CONSTRUCTED AND A NATURAL SALT MARSH OF SAN DIEGO BAY

RENÉ LANGIS, MALGORZATA ZALEJKO, AND JOY B. ZEDLER
Pacific Estuarine Research Laboratory, Department of Biology, San Diego State University, San Diego, California 92182-0057 USA

Abstract. Soil nitrogen pools were lower in a 4-yr-old constructed salt marsh than in an adjacent natural marsh of San Diego Bay. Aboveground biomass and foliar nitrogen content of Spartina foliosa were both lower for the constructed marsh. Soil organic carbon, which was highly positively correlated with total nitrogen, was also lower in the constructed marsh. Rates of nitrogen fixation were higher for the natural marsh in surface soils (1 cm depth) but not in the rhizosphere (10 cm depth). Experimental additions of organic matter increased rates of nitrogen fixation substantially for both the constructed and natural marsh soils, with glucose stimulating greater increases than Spartina foliosa detritus (roots and rhizomes). In comparison with natural marshes studied elsewhere, the San Diego Bay sites have low nitrogen pools and little soil organic carbon. Nitrogen mineralization rates (in situ incubations) were high in both marshes studied. The low nitrogen pools reflect low tidal import and infrequent streamflow influxes and, possibly, high nitrogen demands of vegetation stressed by hypersaline soils.

Key words: mitigation; nitrogen; nitrogen fixation; restoration; salt marsh; soils; Southern California; Spartina foliosa.

INTRODUCTION

Industrial, commercial, residential, and recreational developments along the Southern California coast have destroyed >75% of the region’s coastal wetland area. As habitats have shrunk, several wetland-dependent species have become endangered with extinction. Southern California salt marshes have one endangered plant, and several birds and insects that are considered threatened or endangered with extinction. In San Diego County, only 756 ha of coastal wetland remain; they are distributed among 13 wetlands, which range in size from 0.24 to 171.10 ha (S. Lockhart, personal communication of data from National Wetlands Inventory maps).

Habitat losses continue, as developments and highways expand into wetlands. Mitigation for damages includes attempts to restore degraded wetlands and construct new ones. Because the natural wetlands have been so greatly reduced, it is critical that human-modified habitats replace the ecological functions of natural marshes in order to maintain regional biodiversity (Zedler 1988).

The presence and efficient cycling of nutrients is central to the development and maintenance of marshes, whether they are natural or constructed. Of particular importance in coastal marine environments is nitrogen (Valiela and Teal 1979), which is the primary limiting nutrient in many salt marshes (Howarth 1988), including one in Southern California (Covin and Zedler 1988). Nitrogen levels and availability affect marsh plant productivity, standing biomass, diversity, morphology, reproductive potential, abundance of plant species, and nitrogen content of plant biomass (Valiela 1983). These features in turn influence the invertebrate and vertebrate animals of the wetlands. Inadequate supplies of nitrogen are likely to affect total wetland function, by altering the basic ecosystem processes of primary productivity, decomposition, and food chain support.

Although the role of nitrogen is known to be significant in natural wetlands, there is little information on the nutrient dynamics of constructed salt marshes. Two studies (Lindau and Hossner 1981, Craft et al. 1986, 1988a) are exceptions; both document lower nutrient concentrations in the soils of the constructed wetlands, but the authors reached different conclusions regarding the ability of constructed wetlands to achieve nutrient levels of natural systems.

Lindau and Hossner (1981) compared substrate nutrient levels in constructed and natural marshes on the coast of Texas. Their natural wetlands had low soil organic carbon (<1.3% soil dry mass) and nitrogen content (total N < 600 mg/kg), but levels in the constructed marsh were even lower (<0.5% dry mass and <100 mg/kg, respectively). However, over the 16-mo study period, levels of extractable ammonium and phosphorus, total nitrogen, and organic carbon all increased significantly in the constructed marsh. The increase was attributed to the presence of a dike, which allowed suspended matter and associated nutrients to settle over the dredge spoil substrate. Although all nutrient levels, except phosphorus, remained lower in the constructed marsh than in the natural marsh, the steady

</page>

<page number="2">

increases led the authors to believe that the two systems would become comparable in 2–5 yr.

Craft et al. (1986, 1988a) compared total nitrogen, phosphorus, and organic carbon pools in natural and transplanted marsh soils of the North Carolina coast. In most of the natural marshes they studied, the concentrations of organic carbon and nutrients were high (organic C as high as 8.6% and total N up to 1680 mg/kg) compared to the Texas wetlands discussed above. As in Texas, the constructed wetlands in North Carolina had organic matter (≤1.8%) and nutrient levels (total N < 1000 mg/kg) that were lower than in natural marshes. Although the older constructed marshes had higher levels, Craft et al. (1988a) expected constructed marshes to take much longer than 5 yr to match conditions in natural marshes. They predicted that C, N, and P pools associated with macro-organic matter (material retained by a 2-mm mesh sieve) would not approximate levels of the natural marshes for 15–30 yr, and they predicted that the soil nutrient pools would take even longer to develop.

There are few data on the nutrient status of Southern California salt marshes. Studies in Tijuana Estuary suggest that nitrogen levels are low relative to Atlantic and Gulf coast salt marshes. Covin’s (1984) data for inorganic nitrogen suggest low soil nitrogen pools. Winfield (1980) found that the salt marsh filtered inorganic nitrogen from the tidal water, but that the supplies were inadequate for vascular plant and algal needs. He calculated that tidal import could account for only ≈6% of the nitrogen used in marsh primary production. Inflows from the watershed are also limited, since the region’s Mediterranean climate has little rainfall (mean = 25 cm/yr at the coast), which falls during a few storms each year. Although both Winfield (1980) and Covin (1984) indicate that tidal flood waters have high nitrogen content, the runoff moves quickly through the small coastal wetlands. It is thus understandable that the salt marsh vegetation is nitrogen limited, as shown by rapid and significant responses of Spartina foliosa and Salicornia virginica to urea addition (Covin and Zedler 1988).

While nitrogen supplies may be quite limiting for Southern California coastal wetlands, nitrogen demand by the vegetation may be high. The region has high evapotranspiration rates during most of the year; hence, the lower marsh soils are usually hypersaline (35–45 g/kg). Many halophytes are able to allocate nitrogen to the production of nontoxic cytoplasmic osmotica, namely proline and glycinebetaine (Stewart and Lee 1974, Storey and Wyn Jones 1975, Flowers et al. 1977, Wyn Jones et al. 1977). Cavalieri and Huang (1979) observed an increase in proline levels of the salt-marsh grasses, Spartina alterniflora, S. patens, and Distichlis spicata when soil salinity passed a threshold equivalent to that of seawater. Furthermore, Cavalieri (1983) showed that the addition of nitrogen could increase the accumulation of proline and glycinebetaine in S. alterniflora, indicating how strongly the accumulation of these substances is linked to the availability of nitrogen.

If nitrogen demand is high, and inputs from both tidal and stream flows are low, then, either rapid nitrogen recycling or high rates of nitrogen fixation may be necessary to make up the deficit. At Tijuana Estuary, nitrogen-fixing cyanobacteria are abundant in the epibenthic algal mats and have high productivity during the warmest months of the year (Zedler 1982). In addition, there is a fair amount of evidence that indicates that free-living bacteria of the rhizosphere can contribute substantially to nitrogen availability (Patriquin et al. 1983). This implies that the contribution of nitrogen fixation in Southern California could be higher than in East Coast salt marshes, where nitrogen fixation was estimated to be only a small component of total nitrogen input (Howarth et al. 1988).

We initiated a study within San Diego Bay to evaluate the nitrogen pools and rates of nitrogen fixation of constructed and natural salt marsh areas dominated by S. foliosa. Studies were restricted to a single intertidal elevation and to adjacent wetlands, in order to reduce hydrologic differences between the comparison sites. We hypothesized that the natural wetland would have greater concentrations of nitrogen and organic carbon and that the vegetation (biomass and foliar nitrogen) would reflect those differences. Nitrogen pools were examined in the sediment (total nitrogen, extractable ammonium, nitrate–nitrite, and organic carbon) and in pore water (ammonium and nitrate–nitrite). Soil samples were incubated in situ to evaluate the capacity of each marsh to transform organic nitrogen into available nitrogen forms. Nitrogen fixation was assessed in the surface soil (to 1 cm) and in the rhizosphere (to 10 cm). Soil organic carbon levels were measured, and experimental amendments (glucose and detritus) helped determined if microbial nitrogen fixers were limited by carbon supplies. Because an earlier study (Swift 1988) had identified significantly lower organic carbon concentrations in the soils of the constructed marsh, we hypothesized that rates of nitrogen fixation would be lower in the subsurface soils, where heterotrophic bacteria might be energy limited.

MATERIALS AND METHODS

Site description

The study site (Fig. 1) is located on the east side of south San Diego Bay within the Sweetwater Marsh National Wildlife Refuge (32°38′ N, 117°6′ W). The refuge is the largest remaining wetland complex in San Diego Bay; it comprises 128 ha, most of which is salt marsh. The constructed salt marsh, known as the Connector Marsh (CM), covers 4.9 ha of formerly disturbed high marsh, salt flats, and upland terrain. In the fall of 1984, the site was graded to create eight lower marsh islands and surrounding creek banks, which were plant-

</page>

<page number="3">

ed with S. foliosa from January to March 1985. The constructed site was fertilized on four occasions in 1985–1986 with urea (N addition rate 25 g/m²) (H. Hunt, California Department of Transportation, personal communication). Although fine sediments had accumulated in the channels, the marsh soil was characterized as sandy loam and loamy sand in 1987 (Swift 1988). An air photo from ≈1928 indicates that the entire site was part of the alluvial outwash from Sweetwater River. Dredging and filling along the Bayfront, and use of the wetland as a dump site, raised the topography. Removal of fill was accomplished by the California Department of Transportation as mitigation for widening of Interstate Highway 5, immediately east of the study site.

The selection of a reference site was constrained by hydrologic heterogeneity, which is responsible for both within- and between-marsh soil variability (Mitsch and Gosselink 1986). Because differences in tidal and river inflows are known to determine soil salinity and species composition of the region’s salt marshes (Zedler and Beare 1986), we restricted the choice of a reference wetland to a natural marsh immediately north of the constructed wetland. There were no tidal barriers between the northern portion of the Connector Marsh and Paradise Creek, whereas a tide gate separated the northern part of the Connector Marsh from the southern part, and the Sweetwater River separated the Connector Marsh from other natural wetland remnants. As a further precaution, we selected sampling sites for both marshes at the same intertidal elevation (0.43 m NGVD [Naval Geodetic Vertical Datum]), where S. foliosa was dominant.

The Paradise Creek marsh (PC) covers an area of 10 ha of intertidal salt marsh. The vegetation consists primarily of S. virginica intermixed with S. foliosa, with pure stands of S. foliosa at the elevation selected for sampling. Tidal water moves in through one main meandering tidal creek and a series of secondary creeks. At one time, according to a ≈1928 air photo, the marsh had a separate inlet to San Diego Bay. Later filling and development along the Bayfront blocked that inlet, and a channel was dug straight south, along what is now the eastern margin of the Connector Marsh, so that tide waters entered via the Sweetwater River mouth (Fig. 1).

Nutrient functions were assessed over a 17-mo period, from December 1987 to May 1989, when the constructed marsh was 3–4 yr old. Salinities of low marsh interstitial waters were 27–38 g/kg in the constructed marsh and, 23–36 g/kg in the natural marsh.

Sample collection

The patches of Spartina at the prescribed elevation differed in size; thus long (10–12 m) and short (4 m) transects were used. The short transects were used for nitrogen fixation measurements; these patches were more readily accessible, reducing the delay between field sampling and laboratory incubation. Three short transects were established in each wetland. Samples for all other determinations were collected randomly along the long transects. Four long transects were established in CM and three in PC, where there were fewer areas that met the sampling criteria.

Permanent sampling wells (4–5 per long transect, for a total of 15 at PC and 20 at CM) were installed to collect pore water. Rubber stoppers prevented contamination of pore water by surface water during high tides. Redox potential (using a combination electrode with platinum tip and KCl-filled reference portion) was measured directly in the wells. The electrode was standardized with ZoBell’s solution (0.003 mol/L potassium ferricyanide, 0.003 mol/L potassium ferrocyanide, and 0.1 mol/L potassium chloride) having a Eh of +430 mV at 25°C (ZoBell 1946) and measurements corrected to standard hydrogen electrode values by adding +208 mV to redox readings. A drop of water was also removed to measure salinity with a hand-held temperature-compensated refractometer. Water samples were then collected, put on ice, and taken to the laboratory where they were analyzed for NH₄⁺ within 3 h, frozen, and analyzed for NO₃⁻+NO₂⁻ the same week. Since the volume of water in individual wells depended on the level of the water table at the time of collection, sampling was done as soon as possible after high tide so that a volume of at least 20 mL could be taken.
