The relatively large mesh size of the screen was needed to favor rapid interstitial water exchange and minimize clogging. Samples were filtered with Whatman GF/C filter paper before analysis. Pore water was sampled quarterly from September 1988 to May 1989.

Aboveground biomass of S. foliosa was determined by clipping all plants in 0.25-m\(^2\) quadrats in July 1989. Three quadrats were randomly selected along each of the long transects. Foliar nitrogen and phosphorus were determined so that N:P ratios could later be estimated as indicators of nitrogen limitation.

Sediment cores (5 cm diameter by 8 cm deep, five per transect) were collected for measurement of total and extractable nitrogen, and organic carbon, using a thin-wall acrylic cylinder. Samples were stored in plastic bags and frozen until they could be analyzed. They were collected in May 1988 and May 1989.

Chemical analyses

Pore water ammonium was determined by the automated phenate method and NO\(_3^-\)+NO\(_2^-\) by the cadmium copper reduction method (APHA 1985). Extractable NH\(_4^+\) and (NO\(_3^-\)+NO\(_2^-\))-N values were obtained by extracting 10 g (wet mass) of a fresh soil sample in 100 mL of 2 mol/L KCl for 1 h and analyzing the extract for NH\(_4^+\) and (NO\(_3^-\)+NO\(_2^-\))-N using the same methods.

Soil water content was estimated by gravimetry and used to calculate all soil chemical contents on a dry mass basis. Bulk density values were used to transform those values to a per volume of soil basis.

Dried samples were analyzed for total Kjeldahl nitrogen (TKN) (APHA 1985) and percent organic carbon by a rapid dichromate oxidation technique (Sims and Haby 1971) after soils were ground with a mortar and pestle and passed through a 2-mm mesh sieve to remove large roots.

Foliar nitrogen and phosphorus were determined on S. foliosa clippings. Plants were washed under deionized water, dried at 60° to constant mass, ground with a Wiley mill, digested by the Kjeldahl method, and the digest analyzed for total nitrogen (APHA 1985) and total phosphorus by the standard molybdate ascorbic acid method (Murphy and Riley 1962).

In situ incubation experiment

We estimated nitrogen mineralization in the field with the buried polyethylene bag technique (Eno 1960). Because plant uptake and leaching of nitrogen is prevented, net mineralization rates can be estimated as the increase in NH\(_4^+\) and NO\(_3^-\)+NO\(_2^-\) (Pastor et al. 1984). Sediment cores (5 cm diameter \(\times\) 8 cm depth) were placed into 0.03 mm thick polyethylene bags; the bags were tied and replaced in their respective holes on 3 May 1988 and covered with \(\approx\) 2 cm of sediment. At the same time another soil core, adjacent to the plastic-enclosed core, was collected and immediately taken to the laboratory for analysis of extractable NH\(_4^+\) and (NO\(_3^-\)+NO\(_2^-\))-N, TKN, and percent organic carbon. A total of 20 bags was installed in CM and 12 in PC along the long transects previously described (see Materials and methods: Sample collection). These polyethylene bags are impermeable to water and permeable to gases such as CO\(_2\) so that constant moisture content can be assured during the incubation while permitting gas exchange (Gordon et al. 1987). On 24 May 1988 the bags were collected and taken back to the laboratory for analysis.

Nitrogen fixation

In addition to the short transects previously described (see Materials and methods: Sample collection), three others were installed across from the northernmost island, on the north bank of CM (Fig. 1). For consistency in comparing marsh areas, results from the north bank are presented separately.

Nitrogen fixation was estimated as nitrogenase activity by the acetylene reduction assay because it is both relatively sensitive and simple to perform (Hardy et al. 1968, Casselman et al. 1981). The other method considered, the \(^{15}\)N assay, is several orders of magnitude less sensitive (Capone 1988) and can require much longer incubation periods to yield meaningful results (Seitzinger and Garber 1987). Nevertheless, the acetylene reduction technique has drawn some criticism, such as the possible effects of contaminating gases associated with acetylene supplies on the metabolism of microorganisms (Hymen and Arp 1987) and the possible stimulating effect of acetylene itself (Topp and Germon 1986). However, since the emphasis of this study was the comparison of two adjacent sites, relative acetylene reduction measures were considered adequate. In addition, because major departures from the stoichiometric 3:1 ratio of moles of C\(_2\)H\(_2\) reduced to moles of N\(_2\) fixed were reported by Seitzinger and Garber (1987) in coastal sediments, nitrogenase activity is expressed as nmoles of C\(_2\)H\(_2\) reduced per surface area.

Samples were collected along short transects randomly selected from dense S. foliosa patches. In the field, two randomly selected sediment cores per transect (10 cm deep by 8 cm in diameter, for root zone nitrogen fixation) were immediately placed upright in 1-L glass mason jars. Each intact core fitted flush against the sides of the jar and had a 300 mL head space. In earlier studies, the highest fixation rates were obtained in the upper 10 cm of soil (Whitney et al. 1975, Hanson 1977, Teal et al. 1979, Casselman et al. 1981) and were attributed to the contribution of photoautotrophs in addition to heterotrophs. Thus, surface cores were also collected. Four small cores (1 cm deep by 3 cm in diameter) were taken within a 20-cm radius of the large cores and carefully placed in 275-mL glass mason jars

</page>

<page number="5">

with tops facing inward (head space of 245 mL). Airtight lids (equipped with a serum stopper) were fitted on all jars, which were taken to the laboratory and acclimated overnight at the incubation temperature of 22° and under a photon flux rate of 10.5 \( \mu \)mol·s\(^{-1}·m^{-2} \). The 1-L jars were entirely covered with aluminum foil to minimize photoautotrophic C\(_2\)H\(_2\) reduction. The next morning, commercial-grade cylinder acetylene (Big 3 Industries, Texas) was added to the jars with a syringe, yielding an atmosphere of 10%. Hyman and Arp (1987) identified several contaminating gases in commercial C\(_2\)H\(_2\), mostly hydrogen and hydrocarbon gases; although these contaminants could affect absolute C\(_2\)H\(_2\) reduction values, their effect on the comparative data of this study could only be minor. The head space gases were mixed by pumping the syringe plunger several times. Gas samples were withdrawn from the jar head space on several occasions after 1.7–5.5 h of incubation. The rates of C\(_2\)H\(_2\) reduction were linear over the whole incubation period. Concentrations of C\(_2\)H\(_2\) and C\(_2\)H\(_4\) were measured with a flame ionization detector on a Varian Vista 6000 gas chromatograph. We injected 1-mL samples onto a 2-m Porapak N column (injector temperature: 85°; carrier gas: nitrogen at a 30 mL/min flow rate; oven temperature: 50°). Rates of C\(_2\)H\(_2\) reduction were calculated as the difference between means of C\(_2\)H\(_4\) concentration measured at two sampling times over that period.

Organic matter amendments

The effect of organic matter additions on the rates of nitrogen fixation was tested using soil samples from three short transects situated in the north bank of CM and in three short transects of PC. The north bank site was chosen because it had low soil organic carbon and was physiographically similar to the PC sites, which were along creek banks. On 2 March 1989, four core samples (1 cm depth, 6.2 cm\(^3\)) were collected from each of three randomly selected areas within each transect and carefully deposited in 275-mL jars. In the laboratory, six jars were amended by equally distributing 2 mL of a freshly prepared glucose solution (10 g/L) to the intact cores with a syringe (final concentration, 2 mg/cm\(^3\) of fresh soil), the cores from six other jars were sprinkled with 1 g of detritus and injected with 2 mL H\(_2\)O (final concentration, 42 mg/cm\(^3\) of fresh soil) and, finally, six other jars (also with four intact cores each) were simply injected with 2 mL H\(_2\)O as controls. Glucose was used to evaluate the effect of a readily available energy source. Detritus, which consisted of dried and ground S. foliosa roots and rhizomes, was used to assess the effect of autochthonous organic matter. Amended and control samples were incubated, and C\(_2\)H\(_2\) reduction was performed as previously described (see Materials and methods: Nitrogen fixation).

Statistical analyses

The data distributions were first tested for normality (Kolmogorov-Smirnov test). Within-marsh differences were tested by analysis of variance when distributions were normal and by the nonparametric Kruskal-Wallis test for nonnormal data. If no significant within-marsh differences were detected, data were pooled and a Student’s t test was applied to the normal data and a Mann-Whitney test to nonnormal data.

Ammonium levels in the pore water (Table 1) were significantly higher in the natural than in the constructed marsh and an order of magnitude higher on every sampling date except May 1989. Ammonia measurements in the natural marsh showed high variability (see standard errors, Table 1).

Levels of pore water \( \mathrm{NO}_3^- + \mathrm{NO}_2^- \) were generally low (Table 1), which was to be expected for PC because of the highly reduced condition of its sediments (Fig. 2). Higher \( \mathrm{NO}_3^- + \mathrm{NO}_2^- \) values were expected in the CM samples given the higher redox values of this marsh. The low values obtained are indicative of that marsh's overall lower nitrogen status. Differences in \( \mathrm{NO}_3^- + \mathrm{NO}_2^- \) concentrations between marshes were significant on two of the four sampling sessions (Table 1).

Sediment analyses

Extractable \( \mathrm{NH}_4^+ \) values from PC were significantly higher than in CM for soil samples collected in May 1988 and 1989 (Table 2). This difference was of the same magnitude (3–4-fold) as for the pore water samples collected in May 1989, when the demand for nitrogen by the rapidly growing S. foliosa was high. The 10× difference in pore water values obtained on other sampling periods likely reflects the richer nitrogen content of PC sediments, which is more easily observed during the periods of lower nitrogen demand in summer, fall, and winter. No measurable levels of \( \mathrm{NO}_3^- + \mathrm{NO}_2^- \) were detected in May 1988, which is indicative of active denitrification or nitrate reduction during that period. Differences in extractable \( \mathrm{NO}_3^- + \mathrm{NO}_2^- \) were not significant in May 1989. Extractable \( \mathrm{NO}_3^- + \mathrm{NO}_2^- \) was, as in the case of pore water, much lower than extractable \( \mathrm{NH}_4^+ \).

This kind of variability is characteristic of soils, and is partly a result of the heterogeneous dispersion of microsites where microbial nitrogen processes (nitrogen fixation, ammonification, and denitrification) occur.

Foliar nitrogen and phosphorus

Total nitrogen contents of aboveground S. foliosa were significantly lower (\( P < .005 \)) in the constructed marsh than in the natural marsh (Table 3). Total foliar phosphorus values were not significantly different (Table 3). Taking into account the difference in biomass values between marshes (Table 3), we calculated standing crop of nutrients for each marsh. Aboveground crops of nitrogen and phosphorus were \( \approx 2-3 \) times higher in the natural marsh (5.93 g/m\(^2\) and 0.67 g/m\(^2\), respectively) than in the constructed marsh (2.11 g/m\(^2\) and 0.30 g/m\(^2\), respectively). The lower foliar N values and the lower standing crop of the constructed marsh are strongly indicative of the poorer nutrient status of CM.

Average N:P molar ratios were higher in PC (19.7) than in CM (15.6), which suggests greater nitrogen limitation in the constructed marsh. Smart and Barko (1980) determined experimentally that S. alterniflora and D. spicata both had the same critical tissue concentrations of foliar nitrogen and phosphorus (i.e., N at 7.3 ± 0.7 g/kg and P at 0.44 ± 0.05 g/kg). The corresponding molar N:P ratio of 36.7 was much higher than the ratios obtained in either PC or CM. This ratio is also higher than the critical nitrogen to critical phosphorus ratio of 16.6 they obtained for a freshwater emergent plant in an earlier experiment (Barko and Smart 1979) and supports the hypothesis that halophytes have a higher need for nitrogen to produce proline and glycinebetaine (Cavalieri and Huang 1981).

In situ incubation

Results of the in situ mineralization experiment (Table 4) showed that, although twice as much nitrogen was mineralized in PC as in CM, the relative increases in ammonium in both marshes were similar (\( \approx 9 \times \)). This indicates that specific mineralization rates were as high in the constructed wetland as in the natural one. Ammonification accounted for almost all of the N mineralization, with net nitrification being much less important. This was to be expected given the low redox conditions of these salt marsh soils (Fig. 2). Levels of nitrates and nitrites were probably kept to low levels, given the high denitrification (Valiela and Teal 1979) and nitrate reduction rates (Nedwell 1982) that are common in salt marsh sediments.

The specific rates of mineralization were too low to cause a significant decrease in percent organic carbon and TKN after 21 d of incubation (Table 4). The increase in ammonium values in both marshes indicates that a significant increase in ammonification can occur without a notable decrease in the organic nitrogen pool, because there were high levels of organic carbon and TKN relative to the inorganic forms of nitrogen.

If we assume specific mineralization rates to remain fairly constant, these results indicate that the supply of inorganic nitrogen to the system could not be limited by the mineralization process per se because specific rates were equivalent. Therefore, the differences in the inorganic nitrogen pools (pore water and extractable nitrogen) should be explained by the difference in labile organic matter pools. In these soils, the labile organic matter fraction likely represents a small portion of total nitrogen or organic matter. Since Spartina density and biomass collected along the same transects (Table 3) were also significantly higher in the natural marsh, plant uptake cannot explain the differences in the inorganic nitrogen content of soils.

than in the CM sites (including north bank) on five out of six series of assays (Table 5a). Only the 13 September assay failed to show a significant difference between sites. These rates account for both heterotrophic and photoautotrophic nitrogen fixation, although the contribution of photoautotrophic nitrogen fixers was probably underestimated because of the low light intensity (10.5 μmol·s⁻¹·m⁻²) under which the samples were incubated. The presence of heterotrophic nitrogen fixers could be inferred by the response of nitrogen-fixing organisms to organic matter amendments (see Results and discussion: Organic matter content and importance). Cyanobacteria, on the other hand, are known to be major nitrogen suppliers among grass stems in salt marshes (Jones 1974, Van Raalte et al. 1974, Carpenter et al. 1978) and were an important part of the productive algal mats found in the nearby Tijuana Estuary (Zedler 1980, 1982).

Results obtained from the 10-cm soil cores, which represented heterotrophic nitrogenase activity in the rhizosphere (they were incubated in the dark), showed a very different pattern. While rates of nitrogen fixation were significantly higher in the natural marsh in December 1987, differences were not significant on the three following assay dates, and rates were significantly higher in the constructed marsh (including north bank) in September 1988.

The different pattern observed between the surface and rhizosphere assays is indicative of the complex interaction of the multiple factors affecting nitrogen fixation in coastal sediments. In the surface cores, we can speculate that higher levels of organic matter in PC stimulate rates of nitrogen fixation. In the deep cores this effect of organic matter was possibly masked by the relatively high levels of soil ammonium in the natural marsh. Ammonium has been shown to inhibit nitrogen fixation in salt marsh sediments and in microflora associated with the rhizosphere (Teal et al. 1979, Casselman et al. 1981, Yoch and Whiting 1986). The high pore water (Table 1) and extractable ammonium values found in PC (Table 2) support this explanation. Casselman et al. (1981) showed that nitrogen fixation was inversely related to extractable ammonium levels; zero rates were measured at NH₄⁺ levels higher than 20 μg/g. In the case of surface cores, ammonium concentrations could be lower than the threshold for the switch-off of nitrogenase activity, be-

Seasonal effects could explain the low rates of nitrogen fixation obtained in the December 1987 deeper cores and to a certain extent in the February 1988 surface cores. Since the assay jars were incubated overnight at 22\( ^\circ \)C, only the effect of temperature on the physiological status of the microbial population at the time of sampling could explain lower rates of nitrogen fixation for the surface and deeper cores. Additional seasonal effects for the 10-cm cores could be linked to the development of the rhizosphere, as the low values of December 1987 correspond with periods of slow plant growth. The stimulatory effect of plant roots on nitrogenase activity is well established (Casselman et al. 1981).

Low annual rates of heterotrophic rates of nitrogen fixation (assuming a 365 d/yr and 24 h/d activity period) in both the constructed and natural marshes (\( \mathrm{C}_2\mathrm{H}_2 \) reduction \( 4.28 \times 10^{-5} \) to \( 5.36 \times 10^{-3} \) mol·m\(^{-2}\)·yr\(^{-1} \)) indicated that nitrogen fixation contributes little to either nitrogen budget. Despite a probable overestimation due to reasons reported in the materials and methods section, these rates were much lower than those reported for Atlantic and Gulf coasts salt marshes (\( \mathrm{C}_2\mathrm{H}_2 \) reduction \( 5.14 \times 10^{-2} \) to \( 10.9 \) mol·m\(^{-2}\)·yr\(^{-1} \)) and reviewed by Howarth et al. (1988).

Organic matter content and importance

Soil organic carbon was consistently higher in the natural marsh (Table 2). In addition, percent organic carbon was highly correlated with total sediment nitrogen (\( r = 0.95 \), Fig. 4), which indicates that organic matter is an important potential source of available nitrogen. We also found a significant correlation with rates of nitrogen fixation (\( r = 0.74 \)); this was expected, given that organic carbon is an essential energy source for nitrogen fixation.

Addition of organic matter in the form of Spartina detritus (roots and rhizomes) had a significant effect on the rates of nitrogen fixation (Fig. 5), showing the importance and potential contribution of organic matter produced belowground. Craft et al. (1988b) used stable carbon isotopes to show that emergent vegetation was the major contributor to marsh soil organic carbon in natural and transplanted estuarine marshes of North Carolina. Since only a small part of the aboveground vegetation was shown to be added to marsh organic carbon, the contribution of rhizomes and roots, which are most dense between 5 and 10 cm depth, is considered to be most important (Oenema and De-Laune 1988). More substantial stimulation of rates of nitrogen fixation was obtained in both marshes when glucose was added to the cores (Fig. 5). This implies that the more refractory detrital organic compounds cannot be utilized by the nitrogen fixers and must be decomposed into simpler compounds. While the assay also showed that both marshes were equally limited in organic matter, the positive response of the constructed marsh indicates how nitrogen cycling might be manipulated by adding organic matter.

Ecological applications

As for the Texas (Lindau and Hossner 1981) and North Carolina studies (Craft et al. 1986, 1988a), the San Diego Bay constructed marsh had lower levels of nutrients and organic carbon than the adjacent natural marsh (Table 6). Although organic carbon and nitrogen levels for natural marshes from the three areas are comparable (Table 6), they are somewhat low when compared with nutrient levels of marshes from Massachusetts, Rhode Island, or Louisiana (Valiela 1983).

Four years after construction and planting with Spartina, the constructed marsh has not developed nutrient pools that are comparable to those of an adjacent natural marsh. The 12-mo study period was not long enough to see significant increases in pore water and extractable ammonium, or in total sediment nitrogen

</page>

<page number="10">

and percent organic carbon. The response of nitrogen fixation to organic matter amendments indicated that the process is energy limited. The mineralization experiment showed that specific microbial activity was similar but that total mineralization was twice as high in the natural marsh. Therefore, low nutrient levels in the constructed marsh result from the poorer organic matter pool of the constructed marsh. Several years will be necessary for soil organic matter in the constructed marsh to reach levels permitting a steady-state supply of mineralized nutrients. In Southern California, where year-round mild temperatures are favorable to high mineralization rates, the accumulation of organic matter will be even slower. In addition, a mineralization model for marsh sediments developed by Morris and Bowden (1986) demonstrated that mature marshes with deep sediments are more efficient at recycling nitrogen and phosphorus than young marshes with shallow sediments.

At some mitigation sites, the soils of constructed marshes have been fertilized with urea to accelerate plant growth. However, pulsed nitrogen additions can have undesirable impacts, such as increased insect herbivory and defoliation, which could set back ecosystem development. Such an event occurred at another San Diego Bay mitigation site, where herbivorous scale insects accompanied the S. foliosa transplants, but the natural control agent (a carnivorous beetle) did not (K. Williams, San Diego State University, personal communication). Incorporation of organic matter before planting should have greater potential, as nitrogen would be supplied gradually with decomposition, and nitrogen fixation processes would develop to sustain supplies.

The question of whether or not constructed wetlands will ever duplicate the nutrient cycling function of natural salt marshes remains. Although we have examined the nitrogen pools of only one constructed marsh, and have limited information on the region's natural marsh remnants, our results suggest that mitigation be undertaken cautiously. Exchanging an acre of constructed wetland for an acre of natural wetland results in a net loss in wetland function. Based on the data for Tijuana Estuary (Winfield 1980, Covin 1984, Covin and Zedler 1988) and Paradise Creek Marsh, we believe that nitrogen supplies and availability are close to critical limits. The likelihood that constructed wetlands will have even lower pools of nitrogen and organic matter means that the nutritional status and productivity of the vegetation in human-made salt marshes will be even more severely limited. These predictions are borne out by the lower biomass and foliar nitrogen concentrations of S. foliosa in CM, compared to PC. Presumably, these differences in the vegetation also affect invertebrate and vertebrate consumers of the CM. A study of epibenthic invertebrates (Rutherford 1989) has documented substantially lower abundances in CM than in PC. Since we do not yet know how long it will take for low-nutrient, inorganic soils to build up sufficient organic matter and nitrogen pools that match those of natural wetlands, the time required for constructed marshes to become functionally equivalent to natural salt marshes cannot be predicted.

If nitrogen fixation, tidal inflows, groundwater, and streamflows are not major components of the nitrogen budget of these Southern California marshes, what is the nitrogen source? The mineralization data suggest that the ecosystem relies on nitrogen recycling. If this is true, then the ecosystem is relying on nitrogen pools that build up very slowly.

Nitrogen sources and net growth efficiency of zooplankton in three Amazon River plume food webs Natalie Loick-Wilde,a,*1 Sarah C. Weber,1 Brandon J. Conroy,2 Douglas G. Capone,3 Victoria J. Coles,4 Patricia M. Medeiros,5 Deborah K. Steinberg,2 Joseph P. Montoya1 1School of Biology at Georgia Institute of Technology, Atlanta, Georgia 2Virginia Institute of Marine Science, College of William & Mary, Gloucester Point, Virginia 3University of Southern California, Los Angeles, California 4University of Maryland Center for Environmental Science, Horn Point Laboratory, Cambridge, Maryland 5Department of Marine Sciences, University of Georgia, Athens, Georgia Abstract The plasticity of nitrogen specific net growth efficiency (NGE) in marine mesozooplankton is currently unresolved, with discordant lines of evidence suggesting that NGE is constant, or that it varies with nitrogen source, food availability, and food quality in marine ecosystems. Specifically, the fate of nitrogen from nitrogen fixation is poorly known. We use \(^{15}\mathrm{N} : \ ^{14}\mathrm{N}\) ratios in plankton in combination with hydrological data, nutrient profiles, and nitrogen fixation rate measurements to investigate the relationship between new nitrogen sources and the nitrogen specific NGE in three plankton communities along the outer Amazon River plume. The NGE of small (200–500 \( \mu \mathrm{m} \)) mesozooplankton was estimated from the \( \delta^{15}\mathrm{N} \) differences between particulate nitrogen and zooplankton using an open system Rayleigh fractionation model. The transfer efficiency of nitrogen among larger (> 500 \( \mu \mathrm{m} \)) mesozooplankton was estimated from the change in \( \delta^{15}\mathrm{N} \) as a function of zooplankton size. The Amazon River was not a significant source of bioavailable nitrogen anywhere in our study region, and subsurface nitrate was the primary new nitrogen source for the outer shelf community, which was dominated by diatoms. N\(_2\) fixation was the principal new nitrogen source at sites of high diatom diazotroph association abundance and at oceanic sites dominated by *Trichodesmium* spp. and *Synechococcus* spp. Although we found clear spatial differences in food quantity, food quality, and diazotroph inputs into mesozooplankton, our data show no significant differences in mesozooplankton nitrogen transfer efficiency and NGE (for latter, mean ± SD: 59 ± 10%) among sites. The movement of new nitrogen through pelagic food webs is critical to marine secondary production and the efficiency of nitrogen transfer may be especially sensitive to changes in phytoplankton community structure associated with climate change (Hutchins et al. 2007; Paerl and Huisman 2008). In zooplankton, the proportion of assimilated nitrogen that is used for growth is called the nitrogen net growth efficiency (NGE), a critical, but poorly constrained parameter in biogeochemical models (Touratier et al. 2001; Anderson et al. 2013; Mitra et al. 2014). A variety of controlled laboratory experiments (Checkley 1980; Berggreen et al. 1988; Kiorboe 1989) suggest that zooplankton NGE is consistently around 45% (Touratier et al. 1999; Touratier et al. 2001), while field studies suggest that NGE is much more variable, ranging from 18% to 72% (Le Borgne 1982 and references therein), and sensitive to food quality as shown by the model of Anderson and Hessen (1995). The movement of nitrogen (N) through the phytoplankton into the mesozooplankton community can be tracked and quantified by means of stable nitrogen isotope analysis (Peterson and Fry 1987). The natural abundance of stable nitrogen isotopes in plankton reflects the sources of N supporting biological production, as well as the physiological processes that may alter isotopic abundance within the ecosystem (Montoya et al. 2002; Martínez Del Rio et al. 2009). The \( \delta^{15}\mathrm{N} \) (\( \%_o \) deviation in \(^{15}\mathrm{N} : \ ^{14}\mathrm{N}\) between a sample and atmospheric N\(_2\)) of mesozooplankton and particulate organic nitrogen (PN) in particular reflect the origin, movement, and transformation of nitrogen in the upper water column (Goering et al. 1990; Fry and Quiñones 1994; Benner et al. 1997). The NGE of mesozooplankton can be estimated from the difference in the \( \delta^{15}\mathrm{N} \) of mesozooplankton and PN (\( \Delta \delta \)) if the physiological processes that fractionate the nitrogen isotopes are accounted for (Montoya 2007; Montoya 2008). The release of \( ^{15}\mathrm{N}\)-depleted ammonium (\( \mathrm{NH}_4^+ \)) through excretion appears to play a pivotal role in enriching an animal’s tissues in \( ^{15}\mathrm{N} \), typically by 2%–4% relative to its diet (Minagawa and Wada 1984; Bada et al. 1989; Gannes et al. 1997). The major factors that can affect \( \mathrm{NH}_4^+ \) excretion rates of ammonotelic (ammonium excreting) zooplankton include temperature, body size, nutritional status, food quality, light, and salinity, whereas the principal feeding mode (e.g., carnivory, herbivory, or detritivory) does not appear to have a strong effect on excretion rate (reviewed by Steinberg and Saba 2008). From a physiological point of view, the increase in \( \delta^{15}\mathrm{N} \) with trophic position (trophic effect) results from the partitioning of assimilated dietary nitrogen between new biomass and \( \mathrm{NH}_4^+ \) excretion (Montoya 2008). In other words, the greater the fraction of assimilated nitrogen released through excretion, the greater the trophic effect and the higher the resulting \( \delta^{15}\mathrm{N} \) of the animal’s biomass. PN and mesozooplankton differ in their turnover times and in the type of information they provide on ecological processes over time scales of hours to weeks (Montoya 2007). The \( \delta^{15}\mathrm{N} \) of PN is sensitive to the sources of N (e.g., nitrate, ammonium, \( \mathrm{N}_2 \)) and the uptake mechanisms supporting production (Minagawa and Wada 1986; Carpenter et al. 1997; Waser et al. 2000). This baseline \( \delta^{15}\mathrm{N} \) can be modified by transient events including phytoplankton blooms driven by the injection of subthermocline nitrate into surface waters or by inputs of regenerated ammonium from heterotrophs (Altabet 1989; Waser et al. 2000). Repeated sampling of PN in the water column and vertical integration of the \( \delta^{15}\mathrm{N} \) of PN can provide a measure of the average isotopic state of the upper water column (Altabet and McCarthy 1985; Montoya et al. 2002; Montoya 2007). The \( \delta^{15}\mathrm{N} \) of zooplankton integrates over longer time scales that reflect animal growth rates, and is, therefore, less sensitive to transient events than the \( \delta^{15}\mathrm{N} \) of PN (Montoya 2007). The difference in \( \delta^{15}\mathrm{N} \) between PN and zooplankton at any time is thus a time-averaged value that reflects the cumulative impact of the animal’s feeding and excretory processes over the animal’s characteristic N turnover time. This in turn provides an estimate of the “time integrated” NGE in the planktonic food web (Montoya 2007). A number of lines of isotopic evidence indicate that the incorporation of nitrogen from diazotrophic (\( \mathrm{N}_2 \)-fixing) phytoplankton into mesozooplankton at oligotrophic sites is highly efficient, and may be more efficient than zooplankton incorporation of nitrogen from phytoplankton supported by nitrate in more eutrophic waters. For the tropical North Atlantic, relevant observations include high in situ incorporation rates of diazotroph nitrogen into mesozooplankton (O’Neil et al. 1995), small differences in \( \delta^{15}\mathrm{N} \) among zooplankton size fractions (Montoya et al. 2002), and correlations between \( \delta^{15}\mathrm{N} \) values of amino acids from *Trichodesmium* and various zooplankton size fractions (McClelland et al. 2003). Furthermore, high in situ diazotroph nitrogen incorporation rates into the amino acid nitrogen of mesozooplankton have been observed in the Baltic Sea (Loick-Wilde et al. 2012). Diverse \( \mathrm{N}_2 \) fixing communities occur in tropical river-ocean systems like the Amazon or Mekong River plumes, where multiple allochthonous and autochthonous nitrogen sources may be important (Voss et al. 2006; Foster et al. 2007; Moisander et al. 2008). In such dynamic systems, a variety of hydrographic (e.g., T, S, nutrient concentrations), biological (e.g., community composition and rates of activity), and biogeochemical (e.g., \( \delta^{15}\mathrm{N} \) and \( \delta^{13}\mathrm{C} \)) measurements provide insight into the dominant organic and inorganic N sources supporting different plankton communities (Fry and Sherr 1984; Voss et al. 2006; Loick et al. 2007). Here, we present a comprehensive set of isotopic measurements of dissolved organic carbon, particulate organic carbon, particulate organic nitrogen, and mesozooplankton collected in the outer Amazon River plume in the context of hydrological, chemical, and biological measurements from the same cruise. A recent paper by Goes et al. (2014) described the phytoplankton biogeography of the Amazon plume system based on data collected during the same cruise, identifying three distinct communities, two of which are driven by \( \mathrm{N}_2 \) fixation, either by “diatom-diazotroph” associations (DDAs), or by colonial cyanobacteria belonging to the genus *Trichodesmium* and unicellular *Synechococcus* spp. The third major phytoplankton community of Goes et al. (2014) is dominated by diatoms that lack diazotrophic symbionts. We test the hypothesis that the NGE of epipelagic mesozooplankton is highest at sites where \( \mathrm{N}_2 \) is the principal new nitrogen source supporting primary production. We first identify and quantify the new nitrogen sources for the upper water column, then estimate and compare mesozooplankton NGE at three sites representative of the three distinct phytoplankton assemblages. *Materials and methods* Samples were collected during the R/V *Knorr* cruise KN197 (22 May 2010–22 June 2010) to the western tropical North Atlantic and outer Amazon River plume (Fig. 1; http://www.rvdata.us/catalog/KN197-08). A Seabird SBE-911 plus CTD-rosette system was used to measure hydrographic properties and collect water samples through the upper water column. Samples for inorganic nutrients (SiO\(_2\), NO\(_3\) + NO\(_2\), and PO\(_4\)) were collected unfiltered from the rosette and analyzed at Fig. 1. Station map along the Amazon River Plume salinity gradient sampled in May 2010–June 2010. Stations selected are focused on those for which the dominant phytoplankton communities according to Goes et al. (2014) were identified as given in the color code. Station 6 and stations close to the shelf for which additional nutrient data was available (12 and 13) are also shown. Zooplankton isotopes were sampled during multiple tows at 10 stations (underlined). sea using a Lachat QuikChem 8000 flow-injection analyzer, with an analytical precision for nitrate plus nitrite of ±0.2 \( \mu \)mol L\(^{-1}\). NH\(_4^+\) concentration was measured at sea fluorometrically according to Taylor et al. (2007), with a precision of ± 0.02 \( \mu \)mol L\(^{-1}\). Suspended particles were collected by gentle pressure filtration of 2–17 L of seawater through pre-combusted (450\(^\circ\)C for 2 h) 47-mm GF/F filters that were dried at 60\(^\circ\)C and stored over desiccant for analysis ashore. For isotopic analysis, filters containing particle samples were trimmed, and cut into quadrants or halves that were pelletized in tin capsules. Filters with uneven distribution of material were first ground to homogenize the sample, weighed, and subsampled for analysis. Zooplankton were collected in oblique tows using a 1-m\(^2\) Multiple Opening-Closing Net and Environmental Sensing System (MOCNESS; 202- \( \mu \)m mesh size) through the upper water column during the day and at night. Typically, the MOCNESS sampling depth intervals in the upper 100 m were: 0–25 m, 25–50 m, 50–100 m or 0–25 m, 25–50 m, 50–75 m, and 75–100 m. Zooplankton samples from each net were split with either a quarter or half of the sample preserved immediately in 4% buffered formaldehyde for taxonomic analysis. The remainder of the samples were size-fractionated using nested sieves with mesh sizes of 5000 \( \mu \)m, 2000 \( \mu \)m, 1000 \( \mu \)m, 500 \( \mu \)m, and 200 \( \mu \)m and then transferred onto preweighed disks of 200 \( \mu \)m Nitex mesh (Steinberg et al. 2012) for biomass and gut pigment measurements, and nitrogen and carbon elemental and isotopic analyses. All plankton size fractions were visually inspected for major taxa present using a stereo microscope (6–60X magnification) before being frozen (–20\(^\circ\)C) at sea. Ashore, these samples were subsequently thawed and dried at 60\(^\circ\)C for 24 h and weighed to determine biomass. The samples were then ground to a fine powder and subsampled for nitrogen and carbon elemental and isotopic analysis. All natural abundance measurements of particulate and zooplankton nitrogen and carbon were made by continuous-flow isotope-ratio mass spectrometry (CF-IRMS) using a Micromass Optima interfaced to a CE NC2500 elemental analyzer. Particulate organic carbon (PC) samples for \( \delta^{13} \)C analysis generally were not acidified, as calcifying organisms were not a significant component of the phytoplankton communities (E. J. Carpenter unpubl. data). All isotope abundances are expressed as \( \delta^{15} \)N values relative to atmospheric N\(_2\) and as \( \delta^{13} \)C values relative to VPDB. Each analytical run included a size series of elemental (methionine) and isotopic (peptone) standards, which provided a check on stability of the instrument and allowed us to remove the contribution of any analytical blank from our isotopic measurements (Montoya 2008). In general our analytical blank was < 0.3 \( \mu \)mol C and < 0.15 \( \mu \)mol N. We conservatively estimate that the overall analytical precisions of our concentration and isotopic measurements are better than ± 0.15 \( \mu \)mol for nitrogen, ± 0.3 \( \mu \)mol for carbon, and ±0.15\(^\circ\) for both \( \delta^{15} \)N and \( \delta^{13} \)C. We estimated mixed layer depths from the maximum in the buoyancy frequency of the water column (Turner 1980). The depth of the nitracline was taken as the shallowest depth where nitrate plus nitrite was found, and was compared to the vertical \( \delta^{15} \)N PN structure associated with the nitrate uptake of phytoplankton (Montoya et al. 1992; Altabet 1996) to identify changes in the nitracline depth associated with the lateral advection of shelf waters along the flow of the river plume. N\(_2\) fixation rates were measured according to Montoya et al. (1996) using \(^{15}\)N\(_2\) gas from Cambridge (98% \(^{15}\)N\(_2\)) with triplicate incubations in 4.6 L Nalgene bottles typically using water from six depths in the upper 100 m of the water Table 1. We note that our estimates of N2 fixation may be conservative due to the time required for equilibration of \( ^{15}N_2 \) gas with the incubation medium (Mohr et al. 2010; Dabundo et al. 2014). Dabundo et al. (2014) also caution that \( ^{15}N \)-ammonium contamination in \( ^{15}N_2 \) gas from Cambridge may lead to an overestimation of N2 fixation rates by 0.0008 nmol L−1 h−1, but we had multiple experiments where \( ^{15}N \) incorporation into biomass was undetectable, especially at ES stations indicating minimal to nonexistent contamination by \( ^{15}N \)-ammonium or other bioavailable N species. Our experimental bottles were incubated under simulated in situ conditions for 24 h, then terminated by gentle pressure filtration (10–15 psi) onto precombusted GF/F filters after passage through a 10 \( \mu \)m prefilter. This filtration scheme produced large (> 10 \( \mu \)m) and small (< 10 \( \mu \)m) size fractions to separate N2 fixation by unicellular and larger diazotrophs like DDAs or Trichodesmium (Agawin et al. 2014 and references therein). Areal N2 fixation rates were calculated by trapezoidal integration from the surface to 100 m depth or to the seafloor, whichever was shallower. Contributions of DOM Samples collected during our cruise for measurement of DON concentrations were damaged during transport (P. L. Yager pers. comm.). We, therefore, use measurements of the concentration and \( \delta^{13}C \) of DOC from the same cruise (Medeiros et al. 2015) to estimate the potential contribution of dissolved organic nitrogen to particles in our investigation area. Specifically, we used the relationship between sea surface salinity and the concentration and \( \delta^{13}C \) of DOC to define the conservative mixing line for \( \delta^{13}C \) DOC after Cai et al. (1988) using the endmember values in Table 1, then applied a literature value for the C: N ratio of Amazon DOM (Hedges et al. 1994) to estimate the potential nitrogen inputs to our study area via transport of DOM. Quantification of diazotroph N in PN and zooplankton We used the “concentration weighted” and depth-integrated \( \delta^{15}N \) of PN (in the following termed \( \delta^{15}N_{NCD} \)) as a proxy for the isotopic composition of the base of the pelagic food web. We carried out a trapezoidal integration from the surface to the depth of the nitracline (Montoya et al. 1992) as follows: \[ \text{Weighted Mean } \delta^{15}N_{NCD} = \frac{\sum ([PN]_i \times \Delta z_i \times \delta^{15}N_i)}{\sum ([PN]_i \times \Delta z_i)} \] where [PN]i represents the particulate nitrogen concentration (\( \mu \)mol L−1), \( \delta^{15}N_i \) represents the isotopic composition of suspended particles, and \( \Delta z_i \) is the depth interval (m) represented by sample i. The individual layers, of thickness \( \Delta z \), were bounded by the midpoints between sample depths, and the integration extended from the surface to the nutricline depth. At stations that showed changes in water masses during extended PN and zooplankton sampling (Stas. 2, 6, 19, 20, 23, 25, and 27, see Supporting Information Fig. S1 for water mass analysis), we used the PN profile from the CTD cast that was nearest in time to the MOCNESS tow for comparison to zooplankton. We used zooplankton from the 0–25 m and the 25–50 m depth strata to estimate the contribution of diazotroph N to the planktonic food web. This approach should minimize the potential impact of isotopically enriched particles from below the nitracline, providing a robust estimate of the inputs of diazotroph N in the surface mixed layer (Altabet 1989; Landrum et al. 2011). The diazotroph N contribution was calculated for both particles and mesozooplankton using the isotope mass balance approach of Montoya et al. (2002). The contribution of diazotroph nitrogen to suspended particles was calculated as: \[ \% \text{ Diazotroph } N = 100 \times \left( \frac{\delta^{15}N_{NCD} - \delta^{15}N_{Nitrate}}{\delta^{15}N_{Diazo} - \delta^{15}N_{Nitrate}} \right) \] where \( \delta^{15}N_{NCD} \) is the weighted mean \( \delta^{15}N_{PN} \) of PN calculated using Eq. 1, \( \delta^{15}N_{Nitrate} \) is the isotopic endmember of 4.5‰ for deep-water nitrate (Knapp et al. 2008), and \( \delta^{15}N_{Diazo} \) is the isotopic endmember of −2‰ for N2 fixation into particles (Montoya et al. 2002). The contribution of diazotroph nitrogen to mesozooplankton biomass was calculated as: \[ \% \text{ Diazotroph } N = 100 \times \left( \frac{\delta^{15}N_{Zoo} - \delta^{15}N_{Reference\ Zoo}}{\delta^{15}N_{Diazo} - \delta^{15}N_{Reference\ Zoo}} \right) \] where \( \delta^{15}N_{Zoo} \) is the \( \delta^{15}N \) value of one of the five zooplankton size fractions collected from each depth interval sampled, \( \delta^{15}N_{Diazo} \) is the isotopic endmember of −2‰ for diazotrophic N, and \( \delta^{15}N_{Reference\ Zoo} \) is a reference \( \delta^{15}N \) for zooplankton collected in regions not heavily influenced by consumption of diazotroph nitrogen as described by Landrum et al. (2011). These reference values provide an index to the scaling of \( \delta^{15}N \) with animal size, and the low reference values we used provide a conservative estimate of the diazotroph contribution to biomass. Estimation of the nitrogen specific net growth efficiency We used an open system Rayleigh fractionation model for the steady state case where the amount of N incorporated through feeding is equal to the amount of N lost through excretion as described by Montoya (2007). We are focusing on the steady state by minimizing the impact of the natural temporal variability in \( \delta^{15}N \) by eliminating all stations with evidence for recent changes in \( \delta^{15}N \) and estimated NGE only for stations where the observed variability of the \( \delta^{15}N \) PN values above the nitracline and the zooplankton \( \delta^{15}N \) values from the 0–25 m and the 25–50 m depth strata was < 1‰. At steady state, we then look at the partitioning of isotopes required to produce the enrichment in \( ^{15}N \) we observe in the zooplankton size fractions under the assumption that excretion is the only process that significantly affects the \( \Delta\delta^{15}N \) that we measured: \[ \delta^{15}N_{Zoo} = \delta^{15}N_{NCD} - \varepsilon \times \ln f \] where \( \delta^{15}N_{Zoo} \) is the \( \delta^{15}N \) value of the smallest zooplankton size fraction (200–500 \( \mu \)m) in a specific depth stratum (50–25 m or 25–0 m), \( \varepsilon \) is the isotopic enrichment factor of −2.7‰ for NH\(_4^+\) excretion by zooplankton (Checkley and Miller 1989), and \( \delta^{15}N_{NCD} \) is the weighted mean \( \delta^{15}N \) of PN between the surface and the nitracline (Eq. 1). Equation 4 can be rearranged to yield an expression for \( f \), the fraction of assimilated nitrogen remaining in the animal’s body: \[ f = \exp \left( \frac{\delta^{15}N_{NCD} - \delta^{15}N_{Zoo}}{\varepsilon} \right) \] which is equivalent to the NGE of the animal. Using a value of \( \varepsilon = -2.7\% \) and an isotopic difference (\( \Delta\delta^{15}N = \delta^{15}N_{NCD} - \delta^{15}N_{Zoo} \)) of 3‰, for example, implies a NGE of 0.33% or 33%. Note that the substrate pool for deamination and excretion in an actively feeding animal would be weighted toward the food consumed. Under these conditions, an animal will release NH\(_4^+\) with a \( \delta^{15}N \) lower than that of the food consumed and more than 2.7‰ lower than the \( \delta^{15}N \) of the animal’s tissues (Frazer et al. 1997). Therefore, this simple approach provides an upper limit for the overall efficiency of transfer of nitrogen through the food web to a particular size fraction of zooplankton (Montoya 2007). For more complex situations with time-varying diet, we refer to the Ramesh-Singh model (Ramesh and Singh 2010). For larger zooplankton (size fractions > 500 \( \mu \)m), we used the slopes of the linear regressions of \( \delta^{15}N_{Zoo} \) as a function of size as an index to N transfer efficiency among the different zooplankton size fractions from the upper 50 m as in Montoya et al. (2002). Results Goes et al. (2014) identified three distinct phytoplankton communities separated largely on the basis of salinity gradients across the plume (Fig. 1). These three assemblages included an Estuarine Type (ES) Community located upstream of the plume on the shelf at salinities below 28 and comprised of a high biomass mixed population of diatoms, dinoflagellates, cryptophytes, and green-water *Synechococcus* spp. A second, coastal Mesohaline (MH) Community was located in the northwestern region of the plume off the shelf at salinities between 28 and 35 and contained abundant Diatom-Diazotroph Associations (DDAs, mostly *Hemiaulus* sp./*Richelia* sp.). The third, Oceanic (OC) Community was dominated by *Trichodesmium* spp. and oceanic *Synechococcus* spp. in the oligotrophic offshore waters outside of the plume with salinities above 35. DDAs, *Trichodesmium* spp., and *Synechococcus* spp. are all capable of N\(_2\) fixation (Mitsui et al. 1986; Carpenter and Capone 2008), while the dominant phytoplankton in the Estuarine Type Community must rely on other N sources for growth. We additionally separated the MH community into two subgroups, MH1 and MH2. These two MH groups differed in multiple ways, including their nutrient concentrations (MH1 > MH2, Table 2), DDA cell abundance at the surface (MH1 \( \ll \) MH2), and the relatively low abundances or absence of asymbiotic diatoms at MH2 stations (Goes et al. 2014). Station 23 was unique in that it was the only station with moderate DDA abundances and high N\(_2\) fixation rates despite having low salinity comparable to shelf waters at ES stations, and, therefore, is listed separately in Table 2. Station 21 had a sea surface salinity below 35 (33.6) but was dominated by *Trichodesmium* spp. and oceanic *Synechococcus* spp. according to Goes et al. (2014), and therefore was also listed separately in Table 2. Station 6 was not included in the study of Goes et al. (2014) but was characteristic of an OC station (Table 2), including dominance by *Trichodesmium* spp. (R. A. Foster unpubl. data) and, therefore, classified as an OC station. Stations 12 and 13 were not classified by Goes et al. (2014) but nutrient data for these two shelf stations were added for a higher resolution of nutrient distribution at ES stations (Figs. 3, 4). Nitrogen sources from the river, subsurface waters, and N\(_2\) fixation The mixed layer and nitracline depths were shallowest at the ES stations on the shelf and deepest at the OC stations (Table 2; Figs. 2A,B). Surface waters (2–10 m) generally were depleted in dissolved inorganic nitrogen (DIN: nitrate, nitrite, ammonium), except at ES Stas. 4, 10, 12, 17 (Fig. 3A), and MH1 Sta. 9 (Fig. 3B), where the nitracline shoaled into surface waters (Figs. 2A, 4A). Discussion The relatively few studies to date that have explored the NGE of zooplankton indicate a clear divergence between nearly constant NGE values measured in controlled laboratory experiments (summarized by Touratier et al. 1999) and variable NGE estimates from field measurements (Le Borgne 1982 and references therein). This discrepancy contributes to large uncertainties regarding the role of zooplankton in biogeochemical cycles (Anderson et al. 2013). Our stable nitrogen isotope approach (Montoya 2007) provides a robust, “time integrated” estimate of the NGEs of mesozooplankton (200–500 \( \mu \mathrm{m} \)) from the outer Amazon River plume and adjacent oceanic waters. Interestingly, our data showed no correlation between mesozooplankton NGE and the contribution of diazotroph nitrogen to particles, food quality as reflected in PN: PC ratios, or food quantity as measured by PN and Chl \( a \) concentrations (not shown). Our findings thus corroborate earlier suggestions from laboratory experiments and modeling exercises that mesozooplankton may adjust their feeding behavior in response to changes in food quality and quantity in order to maintain constant nitrogen specific net growth efficiencies and elemental (C: N) ratios in their tissues. Besides the river plume, the onshore advection of nutrient rich North Brazilian Current water (Demaster and Pope 1996), and anticyclonic (warm core) and cyclonic (cold core) North Brazilian Current rings (Fratantoni and Richardson 2006) may have a marked impact on the hydrology and biological activity of the shelf and in offshore waters between the equator and 10°N. Previous studies of the nutrient systematics in the Amazon River and its plume have shown nitrogen to be the most limiting nutrient for algal growth in both shelf (Demaster and Pope 1996) and offshore waters (Cooley and Yager 2006; Cooley et al. 2007). The Amazon River carries high concentrations of silicate (14–150 \( \mu \)mol L⁻¹) and phosphate (0.6–0.8 \( \mu \)mol L⁻¹) but nitrate concentrations of 12–23 \( \mu \)mol L⁻¹ are low compared to other large rivers like the Pearl (Cai et al. 2004) or Mississippi Rivers (Dagg et al. 2004), where nitrate concentrations are typically higher than 75 \( \mu \)mol L⁻¹. Within the plume, this nutrient composition leads to strong N limitation of algal growth at the outer Amazon shelf (4–5°N) where silicate and phosphate concentrations remain high (Demaster and Pope 1996). Algal blooms are nevertheless present on the outer Amazon shelf during all seasons (summarized by Demaster and Pope 1996). The depletion of dissolved inorganic nitrogen we observed in the river plume (Fig. 3A) and the shoaling of the nitracline into surface waters at the ES stations (Fig. 4A) are both consistent with an important role for advective inputs of nitrate-rich subplume waters in supporting primary production on the shelf.
