At all stations, nitrate was present in the top 1–2 cm sediment depth (Figure 2) and N2 fixation was low close to the sediment-water interface (Figure 5), suggesting a negative correlation of nitrate with N2 fixation by the absence of an ecological niche for diazotrophs (Bertics et al., 2010). This negative relationship was identified statistically (Table 2) and phylogenetically, as denitrifying bacteria did not cluster with nifH gene sequences (Figure 4). Altogether, it seems that denitrification was not related to N2 fixation in the investigated sediments. Remarkably, nifH sequences also clustered with V. diazotrophicus, which reduces nitrate to nitrite and which has previously shown to be capable of N2 fixation (Guerinot et al., 1982). Similar sequences were found in the Peruvian OMZ sediment (Gier et al., 2016) and water column (Löschner et al., 2014). Furthermore, no manganese reducers were detected by the nifH analysis (Figure 4). Ferrous iron accumulation in porewater, an indicator for the microbial iron reduction zone (Vandieken et al., 2006), mostly showed an overlapping distribution with N2 fixation activity at all stations (Figure 5). In accordance with this finding, some nifH gene sequences (2 %) clustered with P. carbinolicus (Figure 4), which uses iron and sulfur as electron acceptors (Lovley et al., 1995). This organism was previously shown to be involved in N2 fixation in subtidal sediments of Narragansett Bay (Rhode Island) (Fulweiler et al., 2013), as well as in bioturbated muddy sand sediments at Catalina Island (California) (Bertics et al., 2010). Most remarkably, the sequences related to P. carbinolicus coincided with a ferrous iron peak at the 412 m (Figure 4) and 1,108 m site (Figure 5), indicating a potential involvement of iron-reducing bacteria in N2 fixation. However, the Pearson correlation analysis did not identify a relationship between vertical profiles of N2 fixation and ferrous iron, and even detected a highly negative correlation for integrated N2 fixation and ferrous iron along with a p < 0.5, pointing to more influential environmental control mechanisms or to more complex interactions. In addition to the known heterotrophs discussed above, we recognized several new nifH clusters in the 18°N depth transect, that have not been identified, yet (Figure 4), highlighting the diversity of diazotrophs in marine sediments. Vertical activity of sulfate reduction and benthic N2 fixation generally overlapped (Figure 5) and integrated rates of both processes revealed similar trends along the depth transect (Figure 6). Overall, the phylogenetic analysis of diazotrophs indicated a potential role of sulfate-reducing bacteria for N2 fixation in Mauritanian sediments. Sequences clustered with several sulfate reducers related to Desulfovibrio spp., which was found earlier to be involved in benthic N2 fixation (Bertics et al., 2013; Fulweiler et al., 2013; Gier et al., 2016). Likewise, nifH gene analysis indicated a potential link between N2 fixation and sulfate reduction in OMZ sediments off Peru (Gier et al., 2016). However, the Pearson correlation coefficient identified only a low positive relationship between the two processes with a p-value of p = 0.43. Moreover, individual peaks of N2 fixation and sulfate reduction often did not match (Figure 5). Our analyses indicate that N2 fixation could be partially associated with sulfate reducers, but at the same time, each process may be influenced by different environmental factors. It should, however, be emphasized that N2 fixation, sulfate reduction, and porewater data were each determined from different replicate MUC cores with a sampling distance of up to 50 cm. Lateral heterogeneity and vertical gradients could obscure the actual correlations. Finally, it should be noted that the addition of acetylene could have induced a shift in the benthic diazotrophic community, as it has been previously demonstrated using high-throughput sequencing of sediments with and without the addition of acetylene (Fulweiler et al., 2015). Nevertheless, we expect that a community shift would rather lead to an underestimation of absolute N2 fixation rates. Effects of Burrowing Organisms on N2 Fixation and Related Processes Burrowing sediment infauna has a significant impact on sediment biogeochemistry through its bioturbating (sediment mixing) and bioirrigating (sediment flushing) activity (Kristensen et al., 2012). Mauritanian sediments <400 m are classified as permeable sands inhabited by burrowing macrofauna (Mosch et al., 2012) whose irrigation activity was quantified, here, using an inert tracer (Figure 3). It should be noted that even though we did not measure bioturbation directly, we expect bioturbation and bioirrigation to be closely coupled (Aller and Aller, 1986; Kristensen, 2000). N2 fixation was repeatedly low in the sediment surface (0–2 cm) and increased only in deeper layers (Figure 5). This observation coincided with the intersection of oxidized water with the seafloor (O2 > 30 μM; up to 123 and 138 μM at 47 and 1,108 m, respectively; Figures 1, 2), and with bioirrigation. These factors together could lead to a relatively deep penetration of O2 into the sediment (Revsbech et al., 1980; Ziebis et al., 1996; Kristensen, 2000; Bertics and Ziebis, 2009). O2 is a known inhibitor of the nitrogenase enzyme (Postgate, 1998; Dixon and Kahn, 2004) and an oxic layer at the sediment surface would potentially suppress N2 fixation activity. The Pearson correlation coefficient points to a low negative relationship between integrated N2 fixation rates and bottom water O2 concentrations, suggesting a potential minor impact of the water column O2 concentrations on diazotrophic activity. Alternatively, several marine diazotrophs have developed strategies to protect the nitrogenase from O2 (Jørgensen, 1977; Krekeler et al., 1998; Cypionka, 2000; Muyzer and Stams, 2008). In contrary to the inhibiting effect of bioirrigation through the introduction of O2, burrowing organisms can also increase microbial activity in sediments by facilitating burial of organic matter (Aller and Aller, 1986; Christensen et al., 2000; Bertics and Ziebis, 2010; Kristensen et al., 2012). In fact, the organic carbon content was found to be one of the most essential environmental factors that control benthic diazotrophs (Hartwig and Stanley, 1978; Jørgensen, 1983; Howarth et al., 1988; Fulweiler et al., 2007; Gier et al., 2016). However, while a positive correlation between N2 fixation and organic carbon content was identified for the Peruvian OMZ sediments (Gier et al., 2016), a negative correlation was detected for Mauritania OMZ sediments (Table 2). The Pearson correlation coefficient results also showed a low to moderate negative relationship between N2 fixation and the C/N ratio (Table 2). In addition, burrowing animals can change redox processes by providing additional electron acceptors into the sediment and thereby creating favorable microniches for benthic diazotrophs (Gundersen and Jørgensen, 1990; Ziebis et al., 1996). The potential removal of ammonium by nitrification may provide favorable microniches for N2 fixation (Wenzhöfer and Glud, 2004; Zorn et al., 2006; Bertics et al., 2010) even in the presence of O2 (Krekeler et al., 1998; Cypionka, 2000; Muyzer and Stams, 2008). Diazotrophs are regarded as being inhibited by high concentrations of NH4+ (Knapp, 2012 and references therein); however, it remains unknown, why N₂ fixation is sometimes still found at high concentrations of a bioavailable inorganic N species despite its high energetically costs (Capone, 1988). Given the many positive effects, bioirrigation can have on N₂ fixation, we expected N₂ fixation to be overall enhanced at stations with high bioirrigation signals and to find niches of N₂ fixation in deeper sediment layers as a result of organic matter burial. Indeed, integrated rates of N₂ fixation were high at the shallow sites (47–236 m) (Figure 6), coinciding with the highest integrated bioirrigation rates (Figure 3B). Additionally, the Pearson correlation coefficient identified a strong positive relationship between N₂ fixation and bioirrigation (Table 2B), but with a p-value of 0.3 (Table S2b) indicating no significance. Moreover, no evidence for microniches of elevated N₂ fixation in deeper sediment layers was found. Only the sulfate reduction peak observed at the 90 m site (8–12 cm, Figure 5) coincided with high bioirrigation at this station and could be a result of organic matter introduction by burrowing activity; however, no anomalies were detected in the profiles for organic matter content or C/N ratio (Figure 2). In fact, the Pearson correlation coefficient found a moderate and strong negative relationship between N₂ fixation and organic matter depth profiles (\( p = -0.45 \)) and integrated rates (\( p = 0.81 \)), respectively, in sediments (Tables 2A,B). In contrast, organic matter and integrated N₂ fixation correlated well in Peruvian OMZ sediments (Gier et al., 2016). However, Peruvian sediments and Mauritanian sediments have different environmental characteristics. While the Peruvian sediments are considered as organic-rich mud with an organic carbon content up to 15 wt% (Dale et al., 2015), Mauritanian sediments are more sandy with lower organic carbon content. Sandy sediments display high metabolic activity with rapid organic carbon oxidation (Boudreau and Westrich, 1984; Huettel et al., 2003). Overall, these results suggest that the organic carbon content and the C/N ratio are not the major factors controlling N₂ fixation in Mauritanian sediments. As another study showed, the increase of organic matter does not necessary lead to an increase of N₂ fixation. Fulweiler et al. (2007) observed a switch from denitrification (N loss) to N₂ fixation (N gain) in the sediments of Narrangaset Bay caused by a lower organic matter deposition to the sediments. The Role of Benthic N₂ Fixation off Mauritania The Mauritanian sediments are regarded as sink for dissolved inorganic N, with denitrification being the main N removal process (Dale et al., 2014). In order to determine the relevance of benthic N₂ fixation in the Mauritanian OMZ, we compared N₂ fixation rates determined in this study with denitrification rates from Dale et al. (2014) and Sokoll et al. (2016). Denitrification by Dale et al. (2014) was investigated along a similar depth transect (18°N) and in similar water depth. Denitrification at the shelf site (98 m) was 1.8 mmol m⁻² d⁻¹, while the rate was 0.2 mmol m⁻² d⁻¹ at the deepest site (1108 m). Benthic integrated N₂ fixation at the corresponding sites was highest (0.15 ± 0.004 mmol m⁻² d⁻¹) on the shelf and lowest (0.08 ± 0.002 mmol m⁻² d⁻¹) at the deepest site. Calculating the above mentioned N source and sink processes, benthic N₂ fixation could compensate for about 8–40% of the N loss between the shelf and the deepest site, respectively. However, in the study by Sokoll et al. (2016) denitrification rates along the 18°N transect were found to be higher at similar water depths (53–787 m) and significantly correlated with grain size, a parameter that was not investigated during our sampling survey. Comparing the highest N₂ fixation (90 m, 0.15 ± 0.004 mmol m⁻² d⁻¹) with the highest denitrification rate (96 m, 4.24 mmol m⁻² d⁻¹; Sokoll et al., 2016), as well as the lowest denitrification (787 m, 0.77 mmol m⁻² d⁻¹; Sokoll et al., 2016) with the corresponding N₂ fixation rate, results in a lower compensation when compared to denitrification rates determined by Dale et al. (2014). According to the findings of Sokoll et al. (2016), benthic N₂ fixation would compensate for only 4–10% of the N loss by denitrification. In summary, diazotrophs in the Mauritanian OMZ sediments may have, at certain sites, a considerable attenuating effect on the loss of fixed N from the benthic environment. Benthic N₂ Fixation in the Upwelling Regions Off Mauritania and Peru As OMZs are predicted to increase globally (Diaz, 2001; Stramma et al., 2008; Keeling et al., 2010), it is crucial to understand their biogeochemical processes and feedbacks and make predictions how relatively oxygenated areas, such as the Mauritanian OMZ, will be affected if O₂ becomes further depleted, as long term trends indicate (Stramma et al., 2008). A comparison between the eastern tropical north Atlantic OMZ off Mauritania and the eastern tropical south Pacific OMZ off Peru (Gier et al., 2016) should aid in our understanding of the magnitude of N₂ fixation rates in O₂ deficient environments and the relevant environmental factors (Table 3). Integrated (0–20 cm) benthic N₂ fixation rates from the Mauritanian upwelling were lower (0.08–0.15 mmol m⁻² d⁻¹) than those reported for the Peruvian OMZ (0.01–0.41 mmol m⁻² d⁻¹). Off Mauritania, N₂ fixation peaked deeper than 2 cm sediment depth, while N₂ fixation off Peru was highest in the surface sediments (0–2 cm). Overall, statistical analysis revealed that benthic diazotrophs off Peru were positively correlated with sulfate reduction and organic matter. Our results from Mauritania instead show that there is no single environmental variable controlling diazotrophs, pointing to more subtle relationships including a positive correlation with sulfate reduction and negative correlation with organic matter content. In addition, the filamentous nitrate-storing sulfide-oxidizing bacteria of the genus Thioploca have been observed to densely colonize Peruvian OMZ sediments (Schulz and Jørgensen, 2001; Sommer et al., 2016). These bacteria perform dissimilatory nitrate reduction to ammonium (DNRA) and prevent the accumulation of sulfide in sediments (Fossing et al., 1995; Zopfi et al., 2001; Bohlen et al., 2011). Thus, sediments off Peru represent a recycling site for dissolved inorganic N, releasing high amounts of ammonium into the water column (Bohlen et al., 2011). The interplay between N₂ fixation in predominantly N-recycling vs. denitrifying sediments deserves further attention in future studies. SUMMARY Our findings add to the growing knowledge of benthic N cycling in upwelling regions and will aid in our understanding of potential environmental factors that control benthic diazotrophs. N₂ fixation occurred throughout the sediment and activity widely coincided with sulfate reduction activity. This result was supported by molecular analysis of the nifH gene, which confirmed the presence of several sulfate-reducing bacteria related to Desulfovibrio spp. Molecular analysis further pointed toward a role of iron-reducing bacteria for benthic diazotrophy and N₂ fixation, which overlapped with the presence of ferrous iron in the sediment porewater. However, none of the above correlations between N₂ fixation and sulfate or iron reduction were supported by statistical analyses. We further found no significant effect of bioirrigation on benthic diazotrophs. Our inability to unambiguously correlate observed biogeochemical and environmental parameters to N₂ fixation highlights that potentially more complex interactions with multiple effects exist in the field. A comparison with denitrification rates from the same study area highlighted the ability of benthic diazotrophs to counteract between 4 and 40% of the benthic N loss. Overall, benthic N₂ fixation in the sediments below the weak Mauritanian OMZ was at least one-third of the predominantly anoxic Peruvian OMZ. Given the many positive effects, bioirrigation can have on N₂ fixation, we expected N₂ fixation to be overall enhanced at stations with high bioirrigation signals and to find niches of N₂ fixation in deeper sediment layers as a result of organic matter burial. Indeed, integrated rates of N₂ fixation were high at the shallow sites (47–236 m) (Figure 6), coinciding with the highest integrated bioirrigation rates (Figure 3B). Additionally, the Pearson correlation coefficient identified a strong positive relationship between N₂ fixation and bioirrigation (Table 2B), but with a p-value of 0.3 (Table S2b) indicating no significance. Moreover, no evidence for microniches of elevated N₂ fixation in deeper sediment layers was found. Only the sulfate reduction peak observed at the 90 m site (8–12 cm, Figure 5) coincided with high bioirrigation at this station and could be a result of organic matter introduction by burrowing activity; however, no anomalies were detected in the profiles for organic matter content or C/N ratio (Figure 2). In fact, the Pearson correlation coefficient found a moderate and strong negative relationship between N₂ fixation and organic matter depth profiles (\( p = -0.45 \)) and integrated rates (\( p = 0.81 \)), respectively, in sediments (Tables 2A,B). In contrast, organic matter and integrated N₂ fixation correlated well in Peruvian OMZ sediments (Gier et al., 2016). However, Peruvian sediments and Mauritanian sediments have different environmental characteristics. While the Peruvian sediments are considered as organic-rich mud with an organic carbon content up to 15 wt% (Dale et al., 2015), Mauritanian sediments are more sandy with lower organic carbon content. Sandy sediments display high metabolic activity with rapid organic carbon oxidation (Boudreau and Westrich, 1984; Huettel et al., 2003). Overall, these results suggest that the organic carbon content and the C/N ratio are not the major factors controlling N₂ fixation in Mauritanian sediments. As another study showed, the increase of organic matter does not necessary lead to an increase of N₂ fixation. Fulweiler et al. (2007) observed a switch from denitrification (N loss) to N₂ fixation (N gain) in the sediments of Narrangaset Bay caused by a lower organic matter deposition to the sediments.

The Role of Benthic N₂ Fixation off Mauritania
The Mauritanian sediments are regarded as sink for dissolved inorganic N, with denitrification being the main N removal process (Dale et al., 2014). In order to determine the relevance of benthic N₂ fixation in the Mauritanian OMZ, we compared N₂ fixation rates determined in this study with denitrification rates from Dale et al. (2014) and Sokoll et al. (2016). Denitrification by Dale et al. (2014) was investigated along a similar depth transect (18°N) and in similar water depth. Denitrification at the shelf site (98 m) was 1.8 mmol m⁻² d⁻¹, while the rate was 0.2 mmol m⁻² d⁻¹ at the deepest site (1108 m). Benthic integrated N₂ fixation at the corresponding sites was highest (0.15 ± 0.004 mmol m⁻² d⁻¹) on the shelf and lowest (0.08 ± 0.002 mmol m⁻² d⁻¹) at the deepest site. Calculating the above mentioned N source and sink processes, benthic N₂ fixation could compensate for about 8–40% of the N loss between the shelf and the deepest site, respectively.

However, in the study by Sokoll et al. (2016) denitrification rates along the 18°N transect were found to be higher at similar water depths (53–787 m) and significantly correlated with grain size, a parameter that was not investigated during our sampling survey. Comparing the highest N₂ fixation (90 m, 0.15 ± 0.004 mmol m⁻² d⁻¹) with the highest denitrification rate (96 m, 4.24 mmol m⁻² d⁻¹; Sokoll et al., 2016), as well as the lowest denitrification (787 m, 0.77 mmol m⁻² d⁻¹; Sokoll et al., 2016) with the corresponding N₂ fixation rate, results in a lower compensation when compared to denitrification rates determined by Dale et al. (2014). According to the findings of Sokoll et al. (2016), benthic N₂ fixation would compensate for only 4–10% of the N loss by denitrification. In summary, diazotrophs in the Mauritanian OMZ sediments may have, at certain sites, a considerable attenuating effect on the loss of fixed N from the benthic environment.

Benthic N₂ Fixation in the Upwelling Regions Off Mauritania and Peru
As OMZs are predicted to increase globally (Diaz, 2001; Stramma et al., 2008; Keeling et al., 2010), it is crucial to understand their biogeochemical processes and feedbacks and make predictions how relatively oxygenated areas, such as the Mauritanian OMZ, will be affected if O₂ becomes further depleted, as long term trends indicate (Stramma et al., 2008). A comparison between the eastern tropical north Atlantic OMZ off Mauritania and the eastern tropical south Pacific OMZ off Peru (Gier et al., 2016) should aid in our understanding of the magnitude of N₂ fixation rates in O₂ deficient environments and the relevant environmental factors (Table 3).

Integrated (0–20 cm) benthic N₂ fixation rates from the Mauritanian upwelling were lower (0.08–0.15 mmol m⁻² d⁻¹) than those reported for the Peruvian OMZ (0.01–0.41 mmol m⁻² d⁻¹). Off Mauritania, N₂ fixation peaked deeper than 2 cm sediment depth, while N₂ fixation off Peru was highest in the surface sediments (0–2 cm). Overall, statistical analysis revealed that benthic diazotrophs off Peru were positively correlated with sulfate reduction and organic matter. Our results from Mauritania instead show that there is no single environmental variable controlling diazotrophs, pointing to more subtle relationships including a positive correlation with sulfate reduction and negative correlation with organic matter content. In addition, the filamentous nitrate-storing sulfide-oxidizing bacteria of the genus Thioploca have been observed to densely colonize Peruvian OMZ sediments (Schulz and Jørgensen, 2001; Sommer et al., 2016). These bacteria perform dissimilatory nitrate reduction to ammonium (DNRA) and prevent the accumulation of sulfide in sediments (Fossing et al., 1995; Zopfi et al., 2001; Bohlen et al., 2011). Thus, sediments off Peru represent a recycling site for dissolved inorganic N, releasing high amounts of ammonium into the water column (Bohlen et al., 2011). The interplay between N₂ fixation in predominantly N-recycling vs. denitrifying sediments deserves further attention in future studies.

At all stations, nitrate was present in the top 1–2 cm sediment depth (Figure 2) and N2 fixation was low close to the sediment-water interface (Figure 5), suggesting a negative correlation of nitrate with N2 fixation by the absence of an ecological niche for diazotrophs (Bertics et al., 2010). This negative relationship was identified statistically (Table 2) and phylogenetically, as denitrifying bacteria did not cluster with nifH gene sequences (Figure 4). Altogether, it seems that denitrification was not related to N2 fixation in the investigated sediments. Remarkably, nifH sequences also clustered with V. diazotrophicus, which reduces nitrate to nitrite and which has previously shown to be capable of N2 fixation (Guerinot et al., 1982). Similar sequences were found in the Peruvian OMZ sediment (Gier et al., 2016) and water column (Löschner et al., 2014). Furthermore, no manganese reducers were detected by the nifH analysis (Figure 4).

Ferrous iron accumulation in porewater, an indicator for the microbial iron reduction zone (Vandieken et al., 2006), mostly showed an overlapping distribution with N2 fixation activity at all stations (Figure 5). In accordance with this finding, some nifH gene sequences (2 %) clustered with P. carbinolicus (Figure 4), which uses iron and sulfur as electron acceptors (Lovley et al., 1995). This organism was previously shown to be involved in N2 fixation in subtidal sediments of Narragansett Bay (Rhode Island) (Fulweiler et al., 2013), as well as in bioturbated muddy sand sediments at Catalina Island (California) (Bertics et al., 2010). Most remarkably, the sequences related to P. carbinolicus coincided with a ferrous iron peak at the 412 m (Figure 4) and 1,108 m site (Figure 5), indicating a potential involvement of iron-reducing bacteria in N2 fixation. However, the Pearson correlation analysis did not identify a relationship between vertical profiles of N2 fixation and ferrous iron, and even detected a highly negative correlation for integrated N2 fixation and ferrous iron along with a p < 0.5, pointing to more influential environmental control mechanisms or to more complex interactions. In addition to the known heterotrophs discussed above, we recognized several new nifH clusters in the 18°N depth transect, that have not been identified, yet (Figure 4), highlighting the diversity of diazotrophs in marine sediments.

Vertical activity of sulfate reduction and benthic N2 fixation generally overlapped (Figure 5) and integrated rates of both processes revealed similar trends along the depth transect (Figure 6). Overall, the phylogenetic analysis of diazotrophs indicated a potential role of sulfate-reducing bacteria for N2 fixation in Mauritanian sediments. Sequences clustered with several sulfate reducers related to Desulfovibrio spp., which was found earlier to be involved in benthic N2 fixation (Bertics et al., 2013; Fulweiler et al., 2013; Gier et al., 2016). Likewise, nifH gene analysis indicated a potential link between N2 fixation and sulfate reduction in OMZ sediments off Peru (Gier et al., 2016). However, the Pearson correlation coefficient identified only a low positive relationship between the two processes with a p-value of p = 0.43. Moreover, individual peaks of N2 fixation and sulfate reduction often did not match (Figure 5). Our analyses indicate that N2 fixation could be partially associated with sulfate reducers, but at the same time, each process may be influenced by different environmental factors. It should, however, be emphasized that N2 fixation, sulfate reduction, and porewater data were each determined from different replicate MUC cores with a sampling distance of up to 50 cm. Lateral heterogeneity and vertical gradients could obscure the actual correlations. Finally, it should be noted that the addition of acetylene could have induced a shift in the benthic diazotrophic community, as it has been previously demonstrated using high-throughput sequencing of sediments with and without the addition of acetylene (Fulweiler et al., 2015). Nevertheless, we expect that a community shift would rather lead to an underestimation of absolute N2 fixation rates.

Effects of Burrowing Organisms on N2 Fixation and Related Processes

Burrowing sediment infauna has a significant impact on sediment biogeochemistry through its bioturbating (sediment mixing) and bioirrigating (sediment flushing) activity (Kristensen et al., 2012). Mauritanian sediments <400 m are classified as permeable sands inhabited by burrowing macrofauna (Mosch et al., 2012) whose irrigation activity was quantified, here, using an inert tracer (Figure 3). It should be noted that even though we did not measure bioturbation directly, we expect bioturbation and bioirrigation to be closely coupled (Aller and Aller, 1986; Kristensen, 2000).

Variability in nitrogen uptake and fixation in the oligotrophic waters off the south west coast of Australia

L.J. Twomey, A.M. Waite*, V. Pez, C.B. Pattiaratchi

School of Environmental Systems Engineering, The University of Western Australia, 35 Stirling Hwy, Crawley, Western Australia 6009, Australia

Received 5 December 2005; received in revised form 17 October 2006; accepted 18 October 2006
Available online 6 June 2007

Abstract

The results presented in this study provide the first broad-scale regional characterisation of the phytoplankton-nitrogen dynamics across the continental shelf between the Abrolhos Islands and Cape Leeuwin, Western Australia. We demonstrate key features of N-uptake, including nitrate and ammonium uptake and N fixation, across the dominant current systems of the west coast of Australia during a 2-week period in spring–summer. The surface waters of the region were N impoverished with low phytoplankton biomass. Nitrate and ammonium uptake rates were among the lowest on record, and \( f \)-ratios were high compared to other oligotrophic systems (\( f \)-ratio \( \sim 0.5 \) throughout), indicating an equal preference for nitrate and ammonium uptake. Areas of high phytoplankton biomass were most likely fuelled by nitrate transported into the euphotic zone during temporally short bursts of upwelling on \( \sim \)weekly, rather than monthly time scales. When upwelling had relaxed, phytoplankton productivity was largely maintained by microbial regeneration in the euphotic zone. A large proportion (20–60%) of the phytoplankton biomass was comprised of picoplankton and nanoplankton cyanobacteria. However, rates of \( N_2 \) fixation were 2 orders of magnitude lower than dissolved inorganic N uptake, indicating that \( N_2 \)-fixation did not significantly contribute to phytoplankton productivity during the study.
© 2007 Published by Elsevier Ltd.

Keywords: Phytoplankton; Nitrogen uptake; Nitrogen fixation; Oligotrophic; Western Australia

1. Introduction

Eastern boundary currents are typically associated with upwelling of nutrient-replete water into the euphotic zone, high primary productivity on the continental shelf and rich coastal fisheries (Codispoti, 1983). The oceanographic conditions off the coast of Western Australia (WA) however, are dominated by the Leeuwin Current (LC), which suppresses upwelling, transports nutrient-poor water along the continental shelf and has a negative impact on primary productivity (Hanson et al., 2005b; Pearce, 1991). Consequently, the biological oceanography of the WA coast is unique amongst all other west facing coastlines. The absence of large-scale upwelling, in the presence of upwelling favourable southerly winds, ensures that the coastal waters are oligotrophic and that phytoplankton biomass and primary productivity are low in comparison with upwelling zones. For example, upwelling associated with the Humboldt Current off the west coast of Chile delivers

</page>

<page number="1">

nutrient-rich water to the euphotic zone, which in turn supports high primary productivity and efficient trophic transfer of nutrients to a rich pelagic fishery (Alheit and Bernal, 1993). In contrast, the pelagic fishery off the coast of south-west WA is limited by low primary productivity and commercial fishing is dominated by the benthic rock lobster industry, which is Australia’s largest single species industry (Caputi et al., 2001; Gaughan et al., 2001).

Hanson et al. (2005a, b) showed that waters associated with the LC off the coast of WA were largely devoid of dissolved nitrogen (N). In oligotrophic coastal regions the availability of nutrients, in particular N, dictates the magnitude and spatial extent of phytoplankton productivity (Howarth, 1988). Where the input of new nutrients are limited, phytoplankton productivity is maintained by in situ nutrient regeneration (Howarth, 1988), or where N-fixing organisms are present, through atmospheric N acquisition (Paerl et al., 1981). N-fixing phytoplankton are favoured in tropical and subtropical oligotrophic waters, where N\(_2\) may supply more than 50% of the N demand, which can be equivalent to 50–180% of NO\(_3^-\) supplied from depth (Arrigo, 2005; Capone et al., 2005). In light of these estimates, there is great potential for N-fixing phytoplankton to dominate the community composition in WA waters, where they may supply a large proportion of new N to the euphotic zone.

However, the Capes Current which flows in an equatorial direction and extends in-shore of the LC in the south-west of WA (Pearce and Pattiaratchi, 1999) has been shown to promote upwelling during summer when prevailing wind conditions are favourable (Gersbach et al., 1999; Hanson et al., 2005a, b). Upwelling events extending across the continental shelf width are predicted to occur 5–9 times during the summer (Gersbach et al., 1999), which stimulates phytoplankton productivity. Capes Current waters have significantly higher primary productivity compared to those of the LC (Hanson et al., 2005b). The comparatively higher rates of primary productivity in the Capes Current are largely fuelled by the injection of deep water nitrate into the euphotic zone during short-lived upwelling events (Hanson et al., 2005a, b).

This paper investigates N dynamics associated with phytoplankton communities off the south-west coast of WA. The research was designed to investigate N uptake along the shelf, shelf-break and offshore Indian Ocean waters to determine the relative preference for water-column regenerated N versus upwelled new N, and the relative contribution of N fixation.

2. Methods

The present study was conducted aboard the Australian National Facility R.V. Southern Surveyor (SS09/03) from 24 October to 9 November 2003. The study site was located between the Abrolhos Islands and Cape Leeuwin (ca. 28°S and 36°S) adjacent to the coastline of south-west WA (Fig. 1). Fourteen cross-shelf transects were sampled (A–N) with 10–15 stations on each transect

![Map showing the cross-shelf transects (A–N) and sampling positions between 24 October and 10 November 2003.](page_1012_1042_728_1042.png)

Fig. 1. Map showing the cross-shelf transects (A–N) and sampling positions between 24 October and 10 November 2003.

</page>

<page number="2">

depending on the continental shelf width (total stations = 212). The stations were categorised depending on bottom depth to encompass continental shelf (0–200 m), shelf break (200–300 m) and offshore (300–2000 m) waters. A shipborne acoustic Doppler current profiler (ADCP) enabled measurement of the vertical structure of the currents in 8 m bins to a maximum depth of approximately 300 m.

Hydrographic parameters were collected using a Seabird SBE911 conductivity–temperature–depth (CTD) profiler, fitted with a Seabird SBE32, 24-Niskin bottle rosette sampler. The CTD was equipped with a Licor LI-192SA PAR sensor and a Chelsea Aqua Tracka Fluorometre. Depending on bottom depth, water was collected from between 3 and 15 discrete depths. Dissolved inorganic nutrients (nitrate/nitrite, phosphate and silicate) were analysed onboard with a Lachat Autoanalyser with detections limits of 0.016, 0.01 and 0.15 μM, respectively. Chlorophyll (Chl) \( a \) extraction was performed on 2-L samples filtered onto 25-mm Whatman GF/F filters. Pigments were extracted immediately in 90% acetone following the acidification technique described by Parsons et al. (1984), and read on a Turner Designs TD700 lab fluorometre according to the acidification method of Parsons et al. (1984). For comparative statistics the chlorophyll \( a \) data were transformed (natural log) to satisfy statistical tests of normality and homogeneity of variance. Water samples for ammonium analysis were immediately frozen and stored in the dark until they were returned to the CSIRO Floreat Marine Laboratories. Ammonium analyses were executed on a Lachat autoanalyser using the technique of Kerouel and Aminot (1997) adapted for flow injection by Watson et al. (2004), detect limit \( \sim 0.016 \) μM.

Uptake rates of \( ^{15}\mathrm{N} \) labelled \( \mathrm{NO}_3^- \) and \( \mathrm{NH}_4^+ \) were measured in whole water samples collected from the surface and deep chlorophyll maximum (DCM) depth. Duplicate 500-mL samples were added to acid-washed Nalgene\textregistered{} PET media bottles and incubated within an on-deck incubator with temperature regulation provided by continuous surface seawater flow. Light attenuation for the DCM samples (1% of surface irradiance) was achieved using neutral density screens. The nitrate and ammonium concentrations were unknown at the time of incubation. Therefore experiments were initiated by adding estimated trace amounts (0.05 μM) of \( \mathrm{K}^{15}\mathrm{NO}_3^- \) and \( ^{15}\mathrm{NH}_4\mathrm{Cl} \). Incubations were terminated after 4–6 h of incubation by filtration onto pre-combusted (500 \( ^\circ \mathrm{C} \), 12 h) 25-mm Whatman GF/F filters. The filters were immediately frozen and stored at \( -18 \) \( ^\circ \mathrm{C} \) for later analysis. On return to the laboratory, the filters were dried at 60 \( ^\circ \mathrm{C} \) and sent to the University of California-Davis Stable Isotope Facility for analysis on a Europa Scientific Integra isotope ratio mass spectrometer. Specific uptake (\( v, \ \mathrm{h}^{-1} \)) and absolute uptake (\( \rho, \ \mu\mathrm{M}\ \mathrm{N}\ \mathrm{h}^{-1} \)) rates were calculated according to Dugdale and Goering (1967).

N fixation was measured using the high-precision, high-sensitivity tracer assay described by (Montoya et al., 1996, 2004). Briefly, 4-L acid-washed polycarbonate bottles were filled to overflowing with sample water and sealed with silicon septa caps. A gas-tight syringe was used to deliver 3 mL of \( ^{15}\mathrm{N}_2 \) (98 at% 15N, Sigma Chemicals). The sample bottles were gently mixed and placed in a deck incubator cooled with running seawater. Samples extracted from the DCM were shaded with neutral density screening to approximate in situ light levels, whereas surface samples were not screened. After an incubation period of 6–8 h, particulate material was collected by gentle vacuum filtration (\( <250 \) mmHg) through a filter array that separated the \( \geq 5 \)-μm size fraction onto a 5-μm Nitex screen and enabled the \( < 5 \)-μm size fraction to pass directly onto a 25 mm pre-combusted (500 \( ^\circ \mathrm{C} \), 4 h) glass fibre paper (Whatman GF/F). The \( \geq 5 \)-μm fraction was then rinsed off the Nitex filter with MilliQ ultrapurified water and onto a 25-mm GF/F paper. The filters were immediately frozen and stored at \( -20 \) \( ^\circ \mathrm{C} \) while at sea.

On return to the laboratory, samples were dried at 60 \( ^\circ \mathrm{C} \) and pressed into 5 × 9-mm tin capsules (Costech Analytical Technologies). The samples were analysed with a Roboprep elemental analyser coupled to a Europa PDZ Tracermass Ion Ratio Mass Spectrometer. System calibration was preformed with L-glutamic acid or radish (collegiate) standards. Analytical precision (two standard deviations) of the analyses were 0.5% for PN, 1% for PC, 0.3% for \( \delta^{15}\mathrm{N} \) and 0.15% \( \delta^{13}\mathrm{C} \). The specific uptake rate (\( v, \ \mathrm{h}^{-1} \)) and the absolute uptake rate (\( \rho, \ \mu\mathrm{mol}\ \mathrm{L}^{-1}\ \mathrm{h}^{-1} \)) for N fixation were determined according to the calculations shown in (Montoya et al., 1996).

Samples for phytoplankton taxonomy were collected at \( ^{15}\mathrm{N} \) uptake sites by collecting 500-mL whole seawater samples from the surface (bucket sample) and DCM depth. Each sample was stored in amber glass bottles and preserved with Lugol’s

</page>

<page number="3">

solution. The entire sample was settled and enumerated using an inverted light microscope according to the method of (Utermöhl, 1958). Samples were identified to class level only.

Phytoplankton pigment composition and concentration analysis were taken from 4-L sea-water samples at the surface and DCM. Each sample was collected onto a pre-combusted **(500 °C, 12 h) 25-mm Whatman GF/F filter and immediately stored on liquid N. Samples were sent for analysis at the CSIRO Marine Laboratories, Hobart, for high performance liquid chromatography (HPLC) using methods analogous to those reported by Thompson et al., 2007. Phytoplankton taxa were separated using the CHEMTAX software (Mackey et al., 1996). The initial CHEMTAX pigment ratios were representative of equatorial species (Mackey et al., 1996) and provided strong agreement with the field data (<1% deviation for all pigments used). The following pigments were used for development of the CHEMTAX pigment ratios; peridinin, 19'-butanoyloxyfucoxanthin, fucoxanthin, 19'-hexanoyloxyfucoxanthin, prasinoxanthin, violaxanthin, diadinoxanthin, alloxanthin, violaxanthin, neoxanthin, lutein, zeaxanthin, chlorophyll b and chlorophyll a. Based on the pigments used in the matrix, the biomass proportion of classes; Prasinophyceae, Dinophyceae, Bacillariophyceae, Cryptophyceae, Haptophyceae, Chlorophyceae and the Cyanobacteria, Synechococcus, were determined.

The CHEMTAX pigment output data were analysed using Plymouth Routines in Multivariate Ecological Research (PRIMER v5) software to evaluate similarity and to create non-metric multi-dimensional scaling (MDS) plots.

3. Results

3.1. Physical water types

Major water masses were identified at each site in the present study on the basis of temperature–salinity (TS) characteristics in the surface 40 m, location of the station (relative to shore) and the current measurements using the shipborne ADCP. Using these techniques four major surface water masses were identified (see also Woo et al., 2006; Hanson et al., 2005a): (1) lower-salinity and warmer LC water along the shelf break close to the 200 m isobath; (2) colder, higher-salinity water associated with Capes Current on the continental shelf in depths <50 m; (3) colder, higher-salinity South Indian Central Water (SICW) located offshore of the LC, defined here as offshore Indian Ocean waters; and, (d) lower-salinity coastal water mass located adjacent the coast between Transects G and J (Fig. 1) and most likely influenced by freshwater run-off.

3.2. Chlorophyll a

The average surface chlorophyll a concentration across the study area was 0.20±0.13 mg chl a m^{-3} (SD), \( n = 42 \). There was no significant difference in surface concentration between sites grouped on the basis of location; those being the continental shelf, shelf break or open ocean (\( P = 0.664, \ n = 244 \)). Similarly, there was no evidence of variation in surface chlorophyll a concentration between transects from North to South (\( P = 0.108, \ n = 244 \)), determined by comparing data between 27°S–30°S, 30°S–33°S and 33°S–36°S; nor was there sufficient evidence of a linear relationship between latitude and chlorophyll a concentration (\( r = 0.09 \)).

A DCM was observed throughout the study area as elevated chlorophyll a concentrations near the seabed at sites on the continental shelf or as clear peaks within the water column at depths between 50 and 110 m. This was clearly evident from the representative fluorescence profiles shown in Fig. 2.

At the DCM the mean chlorophyll a concentration across the study area was 0.41±0.19 mg chl a m^{-3} (SE), \( n = 42 \). Comparison of the pooled surface chlorophyll concentration with the pooled DCM concentration revealed significantly higher levels at depth than at the surface (\( P < 0.001, \ n = 84 \)). The mean chlorophyll a concentration at the DCM was significantly higher at the open-ocean (0.526±0.175 mg chl a m^{-3}) and shelf-break (0.447±0.178 mg chl a m^{-3}) sites than those measured on the continental shelf (0.279±0.158 mg chl a m^{-3}; \( P < 0.001, \ n = 42 \)). Similarly, examination of the DCM in the major water masses revealed that the mean concentration in the LC (0.423±0.19 mg chl a m^{-3}) and offshore Indian Ocean waters (0.537±0.187 mg chl a m^{-3}) was significantly higher than those recorded at sites influenced by the Capes Current (0.277±0.038 mg chl a m^{-3}; \( P < 0.005, \ n = 42 \)). The distribution of chlorophyll a in the DCM was lower at northern latitudes (27°S–30°S; 0.301±0.171 mg chl a m^{-3}) compared with the southern latitudes (30°S–33°S; 0.459±0.21 and 33°S–36°S; 0.337±0.181 mg chl a m^{-3}); however, there was no evidence of a statistical difference at the \( \alpha = 0.05 \) level

Depth-integrated chlorophyll a concentrations ranged from 1.84 to 60.69 mg chl \( a \) m\(^{-2} \), with a mean of 27.7\( \pm \)14 SD (\( n = 209 \)). The lowest concentrations were located at continental shelf sites with depths of <30 m (Fig. 3). The maximum concentrations (45–60 mg chl \( a \) m\(^{-2} \)) were recorded in the vicinity of the Perth Canyon (Figs. 1 and 3, 32°S, 115°E). Elevated concentrations were also observed at the 200–300 m shelf break between latitudes 29.5°S and 32°S.

3.3. DIN concentration

Nitrate concentration measured at sites on the continental shelf was typically below detection (<0.016 \( \mu \)M; Fig. 4). Similarly at the continental shelf break and beyond, nitrate concentrations were below detection in the surface 50 m. The nitricline (0.2 \( \mu \)M) was observed at sites with water depth >50 m and was typically deeper offshore than at the shelf break (Fig. 4). In the euphotic zone (\( \leq 140 \) m) at depths greater than the nitricline, nitrate was in the range of 0.5–2 \( \mu \)M. Nitrate concentration increased rapidly beyond 150 m depth to concentrations of around 30 \( \mu \)M. South of Cape Leeuwin on Transect N, the nitricline was shallower (~50 m) than elsewhere and concentrations >2 \( \mu \)M were evident in the euphotic zone (Fig. 4).

Ammonium concentration was typically below the analytical limits for detection (<0.016 \( \mu \)M) throughout the study area. Fewer than 10% of the 143 samples collected for ammonium analysis were above the detection limit. The distribution of ammonium in the euphotic zone was measured at the 100, 300 and 750 m isobaths on transect A (Fig. 5). These depth profiles indicate low ammonium concentration throughout the water column (below detection) with no discernable pattern with increasing depth.

3.4. N uptake

Based on the measured ammonium and nitrate levels and assuming a minimum concentration of 0.016 \( \mu \)M when levels were below the detection limit, the estimated trace additions represented ~1–25% enrichment. Considering that nearly all of the surface N uptake estimates were conducted on water samples where the concentrations of nitrate and ammonium were below detection, our uptake rates represent potential N uptake by phytoplankton in an enriched environment. Our estimates are therefore most likely representative of the maximum potential uptake, rather than ambient uptake rates in the surface waters.

A summary of nitrate, ammonium and N\(_2\) uptake in the different water masses is provided in Table 1. Absolute ammonium uptake was generally homogeneous throughout the study area (Fig. 6A and B). There was no evidence of a significant difference in absolute ammonium uptake between the surface (1.5\( \pm \)0.19 nmol L\(^{-1}\) h\(^{-1}\)) and DCM (1.9\( \pm \)0.22 nmol L\(^{-1}\) h\(^{-1}\), Mann–Whitney \( U \),

Similarly, there was no significant difference in absolute ammonium uptake in the surface waters of the open-ocean, shelf-break or continental-shelf sites (Table 1, Kruskal–Wallace, \( P = 0.163, n = 42 \)); or in the DCM of the open-ocean, shelf-break or continental shelf sites (Table 1, Kruskal–Wallace, \( P = 0.3, n = 42 \)).

Over the entire study area, absolute nitrate uptake (Fig. 6C and D) was significantly lower in surface waters (\( 1.8 \pm 0.25 \) nmol L\(^{-1}\) h\(^{-1} \)) than at the DCM depth (\( 6.1 \pm 1.98 \) nmol L\(^{-1}\) h\(^{-1} \), Mann–Whitney \( U, P = 0.027, n = 82 \)). At the DCM, the inshore waters had a significantly lower absolute nitrate uptake rate than the open-ocean waters (Table 1, Mann–Whitney \( U, P = 0.03, n = 28 \)). There was significantly higher N\(_2\) fixation at the surface than at the DCM at the \( \alpha = 0.1 \) level (Mann–Whitney \( U, P = 0.056, n = 69 \)). 3.5. \( f \)-ratio

Considering that the surface concentration of ammonium and nitrate was most often below the level of detection, the \( f \)-ratio was calculated based on equal amounts of nitrate and ammonium (0.016\( \mu \)M). Given that the absolute uptake values were not resolved at the surface, the calculated \( f \)-ratios represent potential, rather than absolute values. The \( f \)-ratio ranged from 0.11 to 0.95 at the surface and 0.07 and 0.93 at the DCM for all stations (Fig. 8). These data suggest high spatial variability of relative preference for nitrate over ammonium during the study. The mean \( f \)-ratio at the surface was 0.61 (0.18) on the shelf, 0.60 (0.24) at the shelf-break and 0.46 (0.28) at offshore sites (mean\( \pm \)SD). The mean \( f \)-ratio at the DCM was 0.47 (0.20) on the shelf, 0.66 (0.19) at the shelf break and 0.65 (0.18) at offshore sites. This indicates that N uptake was generally equitable between nitrate and ammonium, with a slight bias for nitrate uptake overall. There was an apparent shift from nitrate preference in the surface waters on the shelf and shelf break to ammonium preference at offshore sites; however, this was not statistically significant (Kruskall–Wallis \( P = 0.24, n = 43 \)). Similarly there was no significant difference in \( f \)-ratio between shelf, shelf-break and offshore sites at the DCM (Kruskall–Wallis \( P = 0.08, n = 41 \)) even though there was an apparent trend of nitrate preference at the shelf break and offshore.

3.6. Phytoplankton diagnostic pigment data

MDS plots of the surface and DCM CHEMTAX data indicated approximately 59% similarity (Fig. 9A). The data were therefore divided into two separate communities and were statistically treated on this basis. At the surface two major clusters were identified, with \( \approx 62\% \) similarity (Fig. 9B). The first cluster included 17 of 37 surface samples with sites from the continental shelf break and open ocean. Synechococcus (Cyanobacteria, mean\( \pm \)SD of 60% \( \pm \)12%), haptophytes (12\( \pm \)6%) and chrysophytes (11%\( \pm \)7%) were the major phytoplankton constituents, with diatoms and

<page number="10">

Synechococcus were most abundant in this group (30% \( \pm 6\% \)), while abundances of haptophytes, chrysophytes, prasinophytes and chlorophytes were similar (15% \( \pm 4\% \), 14% \( \pm 6\% \), 12% \( \pm 3\% \) and 15% \( \pm 4\% \), respectively). The combined pigment biomass of diatoms, prochlorophytes, cryptophytes and dinoflagellates represented less than 10% of the total in this cluster.

The phytoplankton community was more similar across all sites at the DCM than at the surface with \( \approx 72\% \) similarity (Fig. 9C). Open-ocean phytoplankton clustered closely together with 91% similarity. Synechococcus, haptophytes and chrysophytes dominated community composition (24% \( \pm 8\% \), 21% \( \pm 7\% \) and 19% \( \pm 8\% \), respectively), with chlorophytes, prasinophytes and prochlorophytes (13% \( \pm 4\% \), 9% \( \pm 10\% \) and 9% \( \pm 8\% \), respectively), while cryptophytes and dinoflagellates comprised <5% of the pigment total in the open-ocean DCM (Fig. 9C). There was greater overlap in the DCM of the continental shelf sites with shelf-break sites, which combined showed 76% similarity (Fig. 9C). These sites had high diversity with the pigment biomass shared equally between Synechococcus, chrysophytes, chlorophytes, prasinophytes, and haptophytes (20% \( \pm 10\% \), 17% \( \pm 8\% \), 16% \( \pm 7\% \), 16% \( \pm 9\% \) and 15% \( \pm 6\% \), respectively). Prasinophytes and haptophytes were less prevalent (7% \( \pm 9\% \) and 5% \( \pm 3\% \)) while prochlorophytes and dinoflagellates comprised <4% of the community pigments. The distribution of phytoplankton taxa as determined by CHEMTAX are shown in Fig. 10A.

3.7. Phytoplankton light microscopy data

Flagellates dominated surface and DCM phytoplankton community of the study area and were largely comprised of dinoflagellates and cryptophytes (Fig. 10B). Diatoms were found throughout the region, with highest proportions in offshore and shelf-break waters in the north (transect A) and on the shelf and shelf-break in the south (transect M). Only a small proportion of the total cell numbers were chlorophytes and chrysophytes, while cyanobacteria were largely absent from the study area.

The relative abundance of the major taxonomic groups was considerably different between the CHEMTAX and the direct cell counting methods. There are two major reasons why these differences were not unexpected: (1) cell counts are a measure of numerical abundance, while CHEMTAX is an estimate of abundance based on major pigment concentration, and (2) microscopy was restricted to cells >5 \( \mu \)m and therefore could not resolve the nano- and pico-plankton fractions, which formed a large fraction of the CHEMTAX biomass (Fig. 10A). Thus the direct counting method is biased toward large phytoplankton such as diatoms, whereas the CHEMTAX method is biased toward those taxa with high concentrations of pigment, yet may under-represent non-pigmented or lightly pigmented groups, such as dinoflagellates.

4. Discussion

In a previous summer cruise, Hanson et al. (2005a) demonstrated that the waters off the central-west coast of Australia were oligotrophic and areas of elevated phytoplankton productivity were associated with sporadic upwelling caused by wind driven processes and the dynamics of coastal currents. LC waters were devoid of N and had low primary productivity, whereas Ningaloo Current and northern Capes Current waters were more productive. The present study across continental shelf of the south-west of Australia suggest that the more southern LC waters off the west coast of Australia have strong similarities with the northern region of the LC. Inorganic N was undetected in the surface waters across the continental shelf and consequently the phytoplankton biomass was low (<20 mg chl \( a \) m\(^{-2}\)). N uptake rates were among the lowest values recorded (<15 nmol L\(^{-1}\) h\(^{-1}\)), comparable to oligotrophic regions of the Sargasso Sea (Glibert et al., 1988).

DCM have previously been described off the west Australian coast (Hanson et al., 2005a, 2007; Thompson et al., 2007) and appear to be a consistent feature of the biological oceanography. Typically DCM are associated with interplay between light and nutrient availability, density structure of the water, and losses to grazing (Cullen, 1982; Tett et al., 2002). In the present study nitrate uptake at the DCM was greater at the offshore Indian-Ocean sites (i.e. those offshore of the LC) than at the continental shelf break, which suggests that the elevated phytoplankton biomass in the DCM was fuelled by nitrate from the deeper waters. In addition, nitrate concentrations at the DCM were typically below analytical detection limits, and the high \( f \)-ratio suggests that nitrate and ammonium were utilised equally. These results indicate a dynamic physiological response that is clearly

integrating temporal and spatial variations in N availability. It was likely that, on average, phytoplankton in the DCM had access to the higher nitrate concentrations, being closer to sources of deep, nitrate rich water. The phytoplankton community would revert to ammonium uptake when nitrate was inaccessible or exhausted from the photic zone. The phytoplankton at the DCM must maintain, therefore, the ability to take up nitrate (i.e., significant cellular concentrations of the enzyme nitrate reductase, or NR) during periods when nitrate is unavailable, such as a time-lag

</page>

<page number="13">

between upwelling events. This would suggest that mixing events occur at a frequency closer to weekly rather than monthly. Longer gaps between nitrate mixing events would allow the deterioration of the NR uptake system critical in maintaining such a high \( f \)-ratio.

Similarly, spatial heterogeneity of integrated chlorophyll biomass observed in this study was related to N availability. For example, high integrated chlorophyll was observed at sites adjacent to Rottnest Island, near Perth Canyon, which has previously been associated with coastal upwelling (Gersbach et al., 1999; Pearce and Pattiaratchi, 1999; Rennie et al., 2007). These results were supported by high nitrate uptake, elevated \( f \)-ratios and a larger proportion of diatoms in the waters adjacent to Rottnest Island compared to other sites. Such observations are consistent with studies of upwelling zones, where diatoms dominate community composition when newly upwelled nitrate is available (Casas et al., 1997; Castro et al., 1994; Wilkerson and Dugdale, 1987). Similarly, the presence of low nitrate concentration combined with elevated uptake is characteristic of biological activity in recently upwelled waters (Dugdale et al., 1990).

However, upwelling on the south-west coast of Australia is sporadic and is predicted to only occur, across the whole shelf, between 5 and 9 times during the summer (Gersbach et al., 1999). The present study indicated that approximately 50% of measured N uptake was attributable to regenerated N in the form of ammonium. Thus, primary productivity in the south-west of Australia is most likely sustained by microbial regeneration of N, previously incorporated by the biological community after an upwelling event. Several studies have shown that when upwelling relaxes, the majority of newly produced organic matter is recycled through the microbial food web, redistributed as ammonium and ultimately reutilised by phytoplankton (Alvarez-Salgado et al., 1997, 2000; Bode et al., 2004). This process often manifests itself as a change in phytoplankton community structure, with nanoplankton and flagellates preferring regenerated N forms, and thereby increasing their relative proportions (Casas et al., 1997; Glibert, 1982; Lipschultz, 1995; Probyn, 1985). High diatom pigment concentration and cell counts on continental shelf sites suggest that diatoms were more prevalent in the Capes Current, which runs northward along the shelf (Gersbach et al., 1999; Pearce and Pattiaratchi, 1999) than in the LC or offshore Indian Ocean waters. The latter two water masses had phytoplankton communities dominated by nano and pico-plankton biomass and large proportions of dinoflagellates and cryptophytes. Owens et al. (1993) demonstrated a strong negative relationship between nitrate concentration and phytoplankton in the \( < 5 \)-µm size fraction. Our results concur, with smaller phytoplankton groups comprising the majority of phytoplankton biomass at sites at the shelf break and offshore Indian Ocean. The prevalence of cryptophytes throughout the region is consistent with oligotrophic waters, where small flagellates are favoured due to their large cell surface to volume ratio and enhanced nutrient uptake rates (Chisholm, 1992). The large number of dinoflagellates observed in our microscopy samples compared to very low concentrations of characteristic diagnostic pigments indicates that the community was largely represented by heterotrophic taxa. The high proportion of heterotrophic organisms, which may also include cryptophytes particularly at the DCM, is consistent with oligotrophic ecosystems where there is a shift from net autotrophy to net heterotrophy under nutrient limiting conditions (Jacobson and Anderson, 1996; Morey-Gaines and Elbrächter, 1987; Sanders et al., 2000).

Our results suggest a highly dynamic coastal phytoplankton community that has developed in response to patchy N supply. This is reflected in the \( f \)-ratio, which was amongst the most variable on record (Planas et al., 1999). Spatial variability of \( f \)-ratio indicates that the phytoplankton community were altering their community structure and physiological response relative to the supply of N. During the austral spring and summer the most likely sources of N for phytoplankton uptake include; regeneration, N-fixation or upwelling delivery from depth via some other episodic perturbation such as a mesoscale eddy (Thompson et al., 2007). Terrestrial N supply was likely to be insignificant during the dry season.

Several studies in upwelling zones have indicated that phytoplankton rely strongly on ammonium regeneration to maintain production throughout the year (Bode et al., 2004; Collos et al., 2003; Mengesha et al., 1999; Varela et al., 2003). The microbial food web plays an important role by recycling a large proportion of the organic material after an upwelling event (Bode et al., 2004). The relative distribution of N in the water column

</page>

<page number="14">

therefore is a function of the time from when the last upwelling event occurred. In the present study, ammonium was below analytical detection limits throughout the study area, yet our estimates of ammonium uptake were highly variable and included some significant uptake rates. It was likely that areas with large proportions of heterotrophic microplankton were supplying ammonium to the autotrophs via regeneration and excretion (Bidigare, 1983; Gaul et al., 1999; Probyn et al., 1990; Whitlege and Packard, 1971). High ammonium uptake is indicative of oligotrophic marine ecosystems (El-Sayed and Turner, 1977; Eppley et al., 1973, 1979; Sharp et al., 1980; Tett et al., 2002) and heterotrophic ammonium supply can account for up to 10–14% of the primary productivity (Bode et al., 2004; Probyn et al., 1990). Our results, which have shown regions with proportionally higher rates of ammonium uptake compared to nitrate uptake, and where ammonium was not detectable in the water column, suggest that ammonium regeneration and uptake are tightly coupled.

It is generally, agreed that the coastal and oceanic ecosystems are critically limited by N (Dugdale and Goering, 1967; Eppley and Sharp, 1975; Eppley et al., 1973; Ryther and Dunstan, 1971), which can lead to an increase of N2-fixing organisms (Paerl, 1990). The filamentous cyanobacterium Trichodesmium has long been considered the primary diazotrophic (N2-fixing) organism in the ocean (Karl et al., 2002). However, more recently the discovery of the enzyme nitrogenase in unicellular, coccoid cyanobacteria and bacteria in the North Pacific central gyre has suggested significant N2 fixation by nanoplankton and picoplankton was possible (Zehr et al., 2001). This was later demonstrated in the oligotrophic subtropical and tropical waters of the Pacific (Montoya et al., 2004). Currently little is known about the global distribution of these organisms, and their contribution to the marine N cycle is yet to be quantified (Arrigo, 2005). However, emerging data suggest that although the distribution of nanoplankton and picoplankton dizotrophs is spatially heterogenous, the rates of N2 fixation can contribute significantly to the total N pool (Montoya et al., 2004).

In N-limited oligotrophic ecosystems fixation can equal or exceed nitrate influx to the euphotic zone (Capone et al., 2005). However, in the present study N2 fixation was 2 orders of magnitude lower than ammonium and nitrate uptake. This was somewhat unexpected due to low rates of ammonium and nitrate uptake and proportionally high pico- and nano-plankton biomass throughout the study area. The low contribution of N2 fixation to total measured N uptake may result from nutrient limitation or co-limitation (Arrigo, 2005). N2 fixation has a strong Fe requirement for synthesis of the enzyme complex nitrogenase (Karl et al., 2002), and reports of Fe limitation of N2 fixation organisms are widespread (cf. Karl et al., 2002). Similarly, limitation by P may also reduce N2 fixation in oligotrophic waters (Voss et al., 2004). Low rates of N2 fixation observed in the present paper are most likely a reflection of severe nutrient impoverishment in the euphotic zone off the south-west coast of Australia. Significantly greater N2 fixation at the surface than at the DCM was most likely due to the high energy requirements of N2 fixation (Karl et al., 2002) and subsequent light limitation of this process at the DCM depth. Additionally, higher nitrate concentration at depth may have inhibited N2 fixation, particularly in Trichodesmium (Ohki et al., 1991). The spatial heterogeneity of N2 fixation observed in the current study indicates that the mechanisms of nutrient supply are the key drivers of N2 fixation off this coast. The sporadic N2 fixation demonstrated here suggests that dizotrophs are most likely reacting to pulsed nutrient supply, either through regeneration or to a lesser extent upwelling.

While only a relatively small fraction of the total measured N uptake could be attributed to N2 fixation in the present study during the austral summer, the presence of nano and pico-plankton dizotrophs off the south-west coast of Australia may indicate that these organisms are more active when the physico-chemical conditions are favourable. Upwelling off this coast has been demonstrated to be strongest during the summer due to upwelling-favourable SW prevailing wind (Gersbach et al., 1999). Nutrient loading to the euphotic zone is profoundly different during winter caused by an increase in terrestrial runoff and changes in wind strength and direction, which have been shown to suppress upwelling through stronger LC flow (Gersbach et al., 1999; Lourey et al., 2006). A better understanding of temporal variability of N2 fixation by nano- and pico-plankton dizotrophs is required to provide a more accurate estimate of their contribution to the N dynamics of the south-west Australian coastal waters.

Additionally, the contribution of N2 fixation by microplankton dizotrophs has not been quantified,

</page>

<page number="15">

even though this region is known to support blooms of chain-forming cyanobacteria from the genus *Trichodesmium*, considered the most prevalent microplankton N$_2$ fixer in the ocean (Carpenter et al., 2004). Senescent aggregation of these microplankton are often observed during the late summer and autumn in WA, such as a bloom estimated at 52,000 km$^2$ on the north-west coast of Australia (Wood, 1965). Considering that the coastal waters of WA are generally oligotrophic, *Trichodesmium* N$_2$ fixation could be an important contributor of new N to the ecosystem; however, quantification of their contribution to the N-pool is complicated by spatial and temporal variability. (One potential reason for the apparent absence of *Trichodesmium* in the oligotrophic waters off WA.)

Although N$_2$ fixation was not a significant source of new N in the study region during the 2-week cruise, the potential for N$_2$ fixation during other seasons may be viable. This was apparent from the HPLC diagnostic pigment results, which showed a large fraction of autotrophic biomass in cyanobacteria. Similarly, the absence of *Trichodesmium* in our microscopy samples suggests that the study may have under represented the N$_2$ fixation potential of the region. However, distribution of *Trichodesmium* may be limited in the oligotrophic waters off the west coast of Australia by seasonal differences in the temperature dependence of oxygen flux, respiration and N$_2$ fixation (Staal et al., 2003). The role of N$_2$ fixation for the biological N dynamics of these waters is therefore complicated by patchy distribution of N$_2$ fixing organisms in space and time, which can only be accurately assessed with greater temporal sampling resolution.

See discussions, stats, and author profiles for this publication at: https://www.researchgate.net/publication/220023193 Fijación de nitrógeno por Cyanoprokaryota en la Reserva Ecológica El Edén, Q.R., México Article in Mexican Studies/Estudios Mexicanos · August 2003 DOI: 10.1525/msem.2003.19.2.277 CITATIONS 3 READS 80 2 authors: Rodrigo Vargas University of Delaware 217 PUBLICATIONS 11,869 CITATIONS SEE PROFILE Eberto Novelo Universidad Nacional Autónoma de México 66 PUBLICATIONS 792 CITATIONS SEE PROFILE Some of the authors of this publication are also working on these related projects: Representantiveness and Design of Environmental Observatory Networks View project FLUCAR View project MEXICAN STUDIES/ESTUDIOS MEXICANOS Fijación de nitrógeno por Cyanoprokaryota en la Reserva Ecológica El Edén, Q.R., México Rodrigo Vargas* Eberto Novelo Universidad Nacional Autónoma de México Acetylene reduction assay (ARA) was applied to determine the rate of nitrogen fixation by cyanoprokaryotes in a wetland in El Edén Ecological Reserve. The data obtained throughout a hydrological cycle showed both an increase of fixed nitrogen during wet periods and an important amount of nitrogen rate produced by non-heterocytic filamentous and colonial blue-green algae. The results support the importance of the contribution of algae to nutrient balance in the wetland ecosystem. Se realizó la prueba de reducción de acetileno para determinar la tasa de fijación de nitrógeno por cianoprokariotes en un humedal tropical de la Reserva Ecológica El Edén. Los datos obtenidos durante un ciclo hidrológico muestran tanto un incremento en el nitrógeno fijado durante el periodo de lluvias como una importante cantidad en la tasa de fijación de nitrógeno producida por algas verde-azules filamentosas no heterocitosa y coloniales. Los resultados respaldan la importancia de la contribución de las algas en el balance de nutrimentos en el humedal. La fijación de nitrógeno no simbiótica por algas cianoprokariotes (Cyanophyta—Cyanobacteria—Cyanoprokaryota) es un hecho bien es- * Trabajo presentado en el Simposio "The Lowland Maya Area: Three Millennia at the Human-Wildland Interface" celebrado en la Universidad de California, Riverside del 18 al 20 de enero de 2001. La realización de esta investigación fue posible gracias al apoyo de UC MEXUS—CONACYT y al proyecto CONACYT 25264-N. También agradecemos al Dr. David Romero del Centro de Investigación sobre Fijación de Nitrógeno de la UNAM por su asesoría y apoyo para la utilización del cromatógrafo de gases. A la Dra. Rosaluz Tavera por su valiosa contribución y comentarios al desarrollo de este proyecto. tablecido y la importancia de esta función en el ciclo biogeoquímico del nitrógeno en los ecosistemas puede resaltarse por la cantidad de nitrógeno que este tipo de algas aportan al suelo. En condiciones de anegación, como en humedales y arrozales, el aporte de nitrógeno al ecosistema puede alcanzar hasta 76.14 nanomoles de etileno por m² por hora (nm C₂H₄ m⁻² h⁻¹) durante la estación seca (Venkatamaran 1981). Para los humedales estacionales tropicales (no arrozales) no existen datos suficientes para comparar la eficiencia de fijación de nitrógeno por las cianoprokariotes pero se sabe que la tasa de fijación de nitrógeno es afectada, en organismos fotosintéticos, principalmente por el suplemento inadecuado de fotosintetatos al sistema de fijación de nitrógeno (Fay 1981). Factores como luz, temperatura, pH y oxígeno influyen directamente en el metabolismo de la fijación de nitrógeno y en el crecimiento de estos organismos (Stewart 1977). Así mismo, la radiación UVB afecta la productividad y disminuye la tasa de fijación de nitrógeno (Falcón-Álvarez 2000; Suresh Babu et al. 1998). Esta función la llevan a cabo organismos heterocitosos y no heterocitosos y puede observarse una separación espacial y temporal de la actividad de la enzima nitrogenasa (Bergman et al. 1997; Paerl et al. 1995; Quesada et al. 1998). En la Reserva Ecológica El Edén existen al menos cuatro meses en los que cerca de una tercera parte de su superficie se inunda. Estas condiciones ambientales dan origen a diversos humedales en donde se desarrollan varios tipos de vegetación en un gradiente relacionado con el tiempo de permanencia de la inundación y la profundidad del agua, desde selva baja subcaducifolia hasta cuerpos de agua permanentes. Uno de los componentes más importantes y menos conocidos de estos ecosistemas es el perifiton que crece en forma rápida y prácticamente cubre todo el suelo y las partes bajas de las plantas. El perifiton está constituido por una red de algas filamentosas y coloniales que forman una trama muy compleja. La productividad orgánica del perifiton en época de lluvias es, probablemente, la más importante de los humedales y desempeña un papel fundamental en el ciclaje de varios nutrimentos (Lampert y Sommer, 1997; MacDougal et al. 1997). Los crecimientos algales de los humedales de la Reserva Ecológica El Edén, están compuestos principalmente por algas de la división Cyanoprokaryota de tipo filamentoso y colonial. Para evaluar cómo es la participación de estas algas en el flujo de nitrógeno en los humedales se analizó la tasa de fijación de este nutriente por estos crecimientos algales durante un ciclo sequía—anegación. Se completa el análisis con una evaluación de la composición relativa de especies heterocitosas, coloniales y no fijadoras en cada caso. Figura 1. Localización de las parcelas estudiadas (1-4) para la evaluación de la fijación de nitrógeno. La zona sombreada señala la zona inundada. Area de estudio La Reserva Ecológica El Edén, Quintana Roo, es parte de la región de Yalahau al noreste de la península de Yucatán. Tiene una elevación entre 5 y 10 msnm y se localiza entre los 21°11"-21°14" N y los 87°10"-87°12" O. Se ubicaron parcelas de estudio (P1, P2, P3 y P4) en 4 sitios de vegetación vascular característica de la Reserva (Figura 1) y en las que los crecimientos de perifiton fueron siempre evidentes como costras compactas y hojuelas subaéreas durante la sequía y como tramas compactas durante el periodo anegado. Métodos Se visitó en tres ocasiones la Reserva durante 2000: abril (secas), agosto (principio de lluvias, periodo anegado) y noviembre (final de lluvias, periodo anegado). Se tomaron cuatro muestras de 1 cm\(^2\) del perifiton (blanco, más tres repeticiones) en cada una de las cuatro parcelas establecidas. Cuando fue posible se recolectó una muestra de agua y se hicieron submuestras dividiendo la costra en superior e inferior para determinar el porcentaje correspondiente de fijación en cada uno de los estratos. Este procedimiento se realizó porque la composición de especies varía tanto en la columna de agua (cuando hay anegación) como en el estrato superior e inferior del perifiton, lo que sugiere una división espacial en la fijación de nitrógeno. Las muestras se incubaron según la técnica de análisis para la reducción del acetileno (Weaver y Danso 1994) y se recolectaron muestras de la evolución de gases (5ml) cada seis horas para cubrir un ciclo de 24 horas. Las muestras de gases fueron almacenadas en Vacutainers y posteriormente analizadas en un cromatógrafo de gases (Varian 3300 y un integrador Varian 4290). Al mismo tiempo, se hicieron observaciones al microscopio de las muestras para obtener la proporción de las formas heterocitosas y no heterocitosas de cianoprokariotes, distinguiendo entre Nostocales y Stigonematales (filamentosas heterocitosas, FH), Oscillatoriales (filamentosas no heterocitosas, FnoH) y Chroococcales (coloniales, Cr) y se registraron como porcentaje de cobertura de un cm\(^2\). Resultados Se obtuvieron valores de la fijación de nitrógeno expresados como nm C\(_2\)H\(_4\) m\(^{-2}\) h\(^{-1}\). Los valores más altos que se obtuvieron corresponden al periodo de lluvias (Cuadro 1, Figura 2). Los estratos del perifiton aportan valores de fijación que se presentan como porcentaje del total obtenido para todo el crecimiento (Cuadro 2, Figura 3). La capa superior es la que produce el aporte mayor en la reducción, aunque resalta el hecho que en la parcela que mantiene menor cantidad de agua (P3), la participación proporcional de los estratos superiores e inferiores es semejante. Los datos obtenidos del agua de las parcelas también son notables pues corroboran el hecho de la pobreza de fitoplancton en El Edén (Novelo y Tavera, en prensa). Por otra parte, los resultados de la proporción de formas de Cyanoprokaryota muestran que las parcelas con mayor tasa de fijación (P4/agosto, P2/agosto y P1/noviembre), no necesariamente corresponden con aquellas con una composición principal de formas heterocitosas, como en la parcela 1 en la que las formas de tipo oscillatorial son los principales componentes del crecimiento (Cuadro 3). Discusión La importancia de la fijación no simbiótica de nitrógeno en sistemas de agua dulce radica en su condición de factor limitante en muchos de estos ambientes (Wetzel 2001). Los principales componentes de la comunidad de algas del perifiton que encontramos en El Edén son las Cyanoprokaryota, que alcanzan cerca del 90% de la cobertura del crecimiento algal. Esta característica no es única de El Edén ya que los tapetes de cianoprokariotes son componentes importantes de los humedales oligotróficos del Caribe (Rejmánková y Komárková 2000). Las formas constitutivas, dentro de este grupo, cambian en las distintas épocas de recolección lo que podría reflejarse en la diferencia en la tasa de fijación de nitrógeno. En El Edén, durante las periodos de sequía (marzo-mayo), el metabolismo de las algas disminuye, se forman estructuras de resistencia y se reduce la tasa de fijación de nitrógeno. Cuando comienzan las lluvias se hidrata el perifiton, el metabolismo algal se activa y se observa un aumento en la tasa de fijación de nitrógeno. En el periodo de mayor anegación es cuando se registra la mayor tasa de fijación de nitrógeno, por ejemplo en las parcelas 2, 3 y 4 en agosto y en la parcela 1 en noviembre. Cuando el nivel de agua disminuye en las parcelas 3 y 4 (noviembre) y el perifiton se encuentra como una costra humedecida, el metabolismo de la fijación disminuye. La presencia de agua, la composición de especies y el cambio en la actividad metabólica después del periodo de sequía es lo que determina el aumento en la fijación de nitrógeno en agosto. Al final de lluvias el estado metabólico del perifiton es distinto ya que aparecen estructuras de resistencia lo que implica una disminución en el metabolismo y por tanto disminuye la fijación de nitrógeno. Este ciclo concuerda con lo discutido por Fay (1981) para los ambientes con ciclos hídricos de sequía y anegación. La fijación de nitrógeno está distribuida verticalmente en la estructura del perifiton (estratos superior e inferior) y en la mayoría de los ca- sos existe una participación similar de cada estrato. Tomando en cuenta que la capa superior está formada principalmente por filamentos de cianoprokariotes heterocitosas y que en la inferior aparecen formas coloniales y filamentosas no heterocitosas, es notable que el aporte de estas capas inferiores sea relativamente importante. La capa superior está formada por varias especies de Scytonema con vainas gruesas y pigmentadas. Esta capa puede servir de filtro a las altas temperaturas, la desecación y como derivado, a mantener temperaturas relativamente menos altas. Estas condiciones favorecerían una condición de baja concentración de oxígeno en las capas inferiores y por tanto la nitrogenasa presente en las células no heterocitosas podría funcionar durante mayor tiempo. Una proporción claramente definida de algas heterocitosas en la estructura del perifiton analizado, durante el periodo de anegación (agosto—noviembre), podría servir como evidencia de que las formas no heterocitosas presentes en la parcela 3 durante todo el año, son las responsables de cerca de la mitad del nitrógeno fijado en ese lugar, sin embargo este hecho deberá ser corroborado con la evaluación de la tasa de fijación en cultivos uniaigales de cada una de las especies predominantes en el perifiton. El Edén presenta un intervalo de fijación de nitrógeno que va desde 2.18 hasta 63.94 nm C2H4 m^{-2} h^{-1} a lo largo del año que puede ser comparado con la tasa de fijación registrada en los estromatolitos de Cyanoprokaryota del lago de Alchichica, Puebla, 0.24 a 25.72 nm C2H4 m^{-2} h^{-1} (Falcón-Alvarez 2000), con la encontrada por Stewart y colaboradores (1978) en varios hábitats de Escocia, que varía entre los 0.02 y 15.7 nm C2H4 m^{-2} h^{-1}, con los valores registrados por Venkatamaran (1981) para los arrozales de la India (76.14 nm C2H4 m^{-2} h^{-1}) y con los de Senegal donde la tasa de fijación varía de 0 a 60 nm C2H4 m^{-2} h^{-1} (Buresh et al. 1980). Esta comparación hace evidente que la producción de nitrógeno fijado por cyanoprokariotes en El Edén es una de las más altas para este tipo de ecosistemas naturales. Los datos obtenidos refuerzan la importancia del papel del perifiton en el ciclo biogeoquímico del nitrógeno, en los humedales en general y en los humedales tropicales en particular, pero sobre todo aclaran el papel de las cianoprokariotes del perifiton en los humedales tropicales cársticos con suelos poco profundos, como en El Edén, donde se mantiene una comunidad vegetal muy productiva.
