In addition to DNRA, assimilation by the microbial community could account for the surplus of nitrate entering the soil. Benthic microphytes are capable of high rates of nitrate uptake, even under dark conditions (Rysgaard and others 1993). Throughout our study, porewater salinities as well as hydrogen sulfide and ammonium concentrations were low and ammonium fluxes highly variable, indicating DNRA was not the dominant sink. The more probable nitrate sink was microbial assimilation. It is plausible that what appears to be excess nitrate taken up by the soil is an underestimate of denitrification due to nitrous oxide (N_2O) production or nitrogen fixation. Denitrification can end in either N_2O or N_2, with the relative proportion depending on soil conditions (Firestone and Tiedje 1979; Knowles 1982). In aquatic systems, nitrous oxide is often a small percent of the nitrogen gas evolved (<10%; Seitzinger and Nixon 1984; Seitzinger 1988; Silvennoinen and others 2008). And although the contribution of nitrous oxide in most coastal Louisiana wetlands exhibits a positive relationship with nitrate concentration (Smith and DeLaune 1983; Lindau and DeLaune 1991), Yu and others (2006) found nitrous oxide was still less than 2% of the nitrogen gas efflux from a coastal wetland receiving diverted Mississippi River water. Because the net N_2 flux as measured by N_2:Ar technique does not account for the production of nitrous oxide (Kana and others 1994), it is possible that nitrous oxide was a significant end-product of nitrate reduction and the denitrification rates presented here are underestimates. As previously mentioned, the N_2:Ar technique only provides an estimate of gross denitrification minus gross nitrogen fixation. Thus, the presence of nitrogen fixation could offset the 1:1 balance of nitrate (NO_3-N) reduced to N_2 (N_2-N) produced. In the spring, when nearly all the nitrate was removed from the overlying water (nitrate concentration: 2 μM), soils in the WLD switched from net denitrification (positive N_2 flux) to net nitrogen fixation (negative N_2 flux). Although it is possible that nitrogen fixation simply “turned on” in the absence of a reactive nitrogen source, the winter net N_2 flux at the Young site was also negative (net nitrogen fixation) under ambient nitrate concentrations of 94 μM. Thus, the disproportional amount of nitrate uptake to N_2 produced may not be the result of an additional nitrate sink, but evidence of nitrogen fixation. Nitrogen fixation is an energetically expensive process and the common paradigm, in aquatic systems, is that fixation only occurs when the availability of reactive nitrogen is low (Howarth and others 1988; Howarth and Marino 2006). However, appreciable rates of nitrogen fixation can occur even when reactive nitrogen is available (Gardner and others 2006; Fulweiler and others 2007; Scott and others 2008; Bertics and others 2010). Furthermore, studies measuring both denitrification and nitrogen fixation demonstrate that these processes can take place simultaneously in aquatic soils and sediments (Gardner and others 2006; Lee and Joye 2006; McCarthy and others 2007; Scott and others 2008). This study provides further evidence that both processes can occur contemporaneously in the presence of reactive nitrogen. Nutrient Biogeochemistry in Deltaic Floodplains Short-term patterns of nutrient accumulation along the 35-year WLD chronosequence were largely consistent with the early stages of soil development described for other types of ecosystems (Crews and others 1995; Wardle and others 2004; Selmants and Hart 2008, 2010). As soils developed in the deltaic floodplain, we observed a significant increase in the molar N:P ratio driven by the accumulation of nitrogen within the soil. Corresponding to the significant increase in soil nitrogen was a significant increase in organic matter (carbon) content. Increasing concentrations of nitrogen and organic matter during soil development have been documented in both natural (Tyler and Zieman 1999; Krull and Craft 2009) and created wetlands (Craft and others 1999, 2002; Anderson and others 2005; Hernandez and Mitsch 2007; Wolf and others 2011). The tight coupling between organic matter (carbon) and nitrogen is expected during wetland ecosystem succession as biological rather than geochemical processes control their accumulation (Craft 1997). In the WLD, the small, but significant increase in soil phosphorus with delta age represents a deviation from classic models of phosphorus dynamics (Walker and Syers 1976; Chapin and others 1994; Selmants and Hart 2010). At the Young site, total phosphorus content (per cm^3 soil) was approximately twofold to fivefold less than measured at the onset of soil development in terrestrial ecosystems and reflects the alluvial nature of substrate formation in the WLD (Chapin and others 1994; Crews and others 1995; Selmants and Hart 2010). However, despite the relatively low initial phosphorus content relative to other types of emerging landscapes, molar N:P ratios throughout the WLD were less than 16, indicating nitrogen limitation according to the Redfield ratio and a N:P ratio of 35 for wetland vegetation and soils (Redfield 1958; Bedford and others 1999). The slight increase observed in total phosphorus, the non-limiting nutrient, suggests that phosphorus dynamics during soil development in the WLD are independent of biological control and regulated by physical (for example, sediment trapping) or geochemical (for example, sorption) processes (Craft 1997; Megonigal and Neubauer 2009). In the present study, short-term patterns of phosphorus accumulation may be attributed to a difference in sediment grain size between the sites. A study conducted in the neighboring Atchafalaya delta observed an inverse relationship between total phosphorus and sediment grain size, with significantly higher phosphorus content in the suspended versus bedload sediment of the river (Poach and Faulkner 2007). Vegetation plays an important role in wetland sediment dynamics by decreasing flow velocities and trapping suspended sediments (Johnson and others 1985; Morris and others 2002). At the older sites, the year-round presence of aboveground vegetation, particularly during periods of high river flow, may capture a larger proportion of fine grain, phosphorus-rich sediments. Classic conceptual models of nutrient dynamics predict nitrogen fixation and atmospheric deposition to increase soil nitrogen content during early ecosystem development (Walker and Syers 1976; Gorham and others 1979; van Cleve and others 1991). Research in terrestrial ecosystems supports this prediction and shows the relative importance of nitrogen fixation to decrease with substrate age (Hobbie and others 1998; Pearson and Vitousek 2002; Schmidt and others 2008). Similarly, rates of nitrogen fixation tend to be greater in newly created or restored marshes relative to more mature wetland systems (Curin and others 1996; Piehler and others 1998; Tyler and others 2003). However, there is no evidence as to how the relationship between nitrogen fixation and substrate age may change under nitrate-enriched conditions. In the current study, net N_2 fluxes under ambient nitrate concentrations (>60 μM) were largely positive. A positive net N_2 flux does not preclude the possibility of nitrogen fixation; it simply indicates greater rates of gross denitrification (direct denitrification + coupled nitrification–denitrification + anammox) than gross nitrogen fixation. Thus, under nitrate-enriched conditions, the dominant N_2 transformation (denitrification) was removing reactive nitrogen from the WLD, rather than increasing nitrogen via fixation as predicted by the classic conceptual models. Denitrification rates in newly created or restored marshes generally exhibit a positive relationship with wetland age (Thompson and others 1995; Currin and others 1996; Hernandez and Mitsch 2007; Wolf and others 2011). The low denitrification rates measured in the coarse soils of newly created wetlands have been attributed to a lack of organic matter and low moisture (Hernandez and Mitsch 2007; Wolf and others 2011). In addition, tidal flushing through these coarse, porous soils may increase porewater oxygen concentrations while simultaneously decreasing available nitrate, thereby decreasing denitrification rates (Thompson and others 1995). Various studies have reported a positive relationship between denitrification and soil organic matter content in wetland ecosystems (Davis and others 2004; Arango and others 2007; Dodla and others 2008; Hopfensperger and others 2009; Wolf and others 2011). Organic matter, specifically labile organic carbon compounds, can directly control the size or activity of the heterotrophic denitrifying population (Groffman 1994). In addition, organic matter can indirectly influence denitrification rates through regulation of soil metabolism, oxygen demand, and nitrogen remineralization (Seitzinger 1988; Cornwell and others 1999). During the winter and spring sampling events, net N_2 fluxes largely paralleled changes in organic matter, with significantly lower (or negative) fluxes occurring at the Young site (Figure 5). However, net N_2 fluxes in the summer/fall were similar across the delta and showed no correlation with organic matter. Summer/fall was the only season vegetation was present in all three sites. Previous studies show enhanced rates of denitrification in vegetated soils due to the leaching of labile organic carbon compounds from the roots of macrophytes and increased oxygen diffusion (via the coupled nitrification–denitrification pathway; Sherr and Payne 1978; Reddy and others 1989; Caffrey and Kemp 1992; Risgaard-Petersen and Jensen 1997). In the WLD, it appears as though the presence of vegetation, particularly in newly emerged substrates, may stimulate denitrification. This suggests that deltaic floodplains, at the mouth of major rivers, have a similar function along the longitudinal dimension of alluvial floodplains in reducing nitrate before river water enters coastal ocean. This function has two temporal dimensions that contribute to the fate of nitrate including age of the delta lobe and seasonal flood-pulse effects of vegetation and flooding frequency. CONCLUSIONS Overall, this study suggests that classic conceptual models of soil development should be applied with caution when describing short-term patterns of nutrient biogeochemistry during the early successional stages of the delta cycle. Throughout the 35-year WLD chronosequence, total nitrogen and organic matter (carbon) content exhibited a positive relationship with delta age similar to the general patterns previously described for both alluvial and terrestrial ecosystems. However, in contrast to these other ecosystems, the mechanisms controlling phosphorus dynamics yielded a slight increase in total phosphorus content as soils within the WLD developed. When using the alluvial floodplain model to predict net N_2 fluxes during delta development, the availability of nitrogen, specifically nitrate, as well as delta age needs to be taken into consideration. Under ambient nitrate concentrations (>60 μM), the net exchange of N_2 gas was largely positive, indicating greater rates of gross denitrification than gross nitrogen fixation. In the absence of nitrate, the net N_2 flux reversed and soils exhibited net fixation. Soil organic matter content in conjunction with the presence of vegetation significantly affected net N_2, oxygen, nitrate, and nitrite fluxes yielding lower fluxes at the Young site (~10 years old). Consequently, as soils in the WLD age, their capacity for nitrate uptake and net denitrification increases. We conclude that early stages of delta development have significant capacity to remove nitrate from river waters as they are transported to nearshore waters. Thus, the formation of a river-dominated deltaic coast will reduce nutrient enrichment as organic matter content in soils increase with vegetative colonization of emerging landscapes. Nutrient Biogeochemistry During the Early Stages of Delta Development in the Mississippi River Deltaic Plain

Kelly M. Henry* and Robert R. Twilley

Department of Oceanography and Coastal Sciences, School of the Coast and Environment, Louisiana State University, Baton Rouge, Louisiana 70803, USA

ABSTRACT

Nutrient biogeochemistry associated with the early stages of soil development in deltaic floodplains has not been well defined. Such a model should follow classic patterns of soil nutrient pools described for alluvial ecosystems that are dominated by mineral matter high in phosphorus and low in carbon and nitrogen. A contrast with classic models of soil development is the anthropogenically enriched high nitrate conditions due to agricultural fertilization in upstream watersheds. Here we determine if short-term patterns of soil chemistry and dissolved inorganic nutrient fluxes along the emerging Wax Lake delta (WLD) chronosequence are consistent with conceptual models of long-term nutrient availability described for other ecosystems. We add a low nitrate treatment more typical of historic delta development to evaluate the role of nitrate enrichment in determining the net dinitrogen (N_2) flux. Throughout the 35-year chronosequence, soil nitrogen and organic matter content significantly increased by an order of magnitude, whereas phosphorus exhibited a less pronounced increase. Under ambient nitrate concentrations (>60 μM), mean net N_2 fluxes (157.5 μmol N m^{-2} h^{-1}) indicated greater rates of gross denitrification than gross nitrogen fixation; however, under low nitrate concentrations (<2 μM), soils switched from net denitrification to net nitrogen fixation (−74.5 μmol N m^{-2} h^{-1}). As soils in the WLD aged, the subsequent increase in organic matter stimulated net N_2, oxygen, nitrate, and nitrite fluxes producing greater fluxes in more mature soils. In conclusion, soil nitrogen and carbon accumulation along an emerging delta chronosequence largely coincide with classic patterns of soil development described for alluvial floodplains, and substrate age together with ambient nitrogen availability can be used to predict net N_2 fluxes during early delta evolution.

Key words: alluvial chronosequence; Atchafalaya basin; benthic fluxes; deltaic floodplain; N_2:Ar technique; nitrogen cycling.

INTRODUCTION

A Biogeochemical Model of Deltaic Floodplains
